features.name: Signal/execution separation via narrow module interfaces
features.description: Signal modules answer only a closed-bar query: direction (+1/0/-1) plus proposed entry price, SL, TP and expiry. Sizing, order handling, trailing and exits live in separate replaceable modules, wired and validated in OnInit. Stateful detectors (FVG, liquidity) own their state and publish events (FORMED, SWEPT, RESET). In MQL5 use a base class with virtual methods; strategy code never calls OrderSend itself.
features.rationale: A clean seam lets the signal be tested with fixed risk rules and the risk/execution layer be tested with a trivial signal, so a strategy change cannot silently break order handling. It adds no tunable parameters. Build a slim own interface rather than adopting the heavy standard-library CExpert shell wholesale (268), which is opaque when something goes wrong.
features.gold_silver_notes: The same execution and risk layer can serve XAUUSD and XAGUSD while only the signal config differs. Signals should propose SL/TP as prices so the executor can apply each metal's stops-level and spread checks before sending.

features.name: One context object per symbol inside a single EA, with shared account-level risk
features.description: One class instance per traded symbol (Init(symbol, params)) holds its own parameters, indicator handles, new-bar state and symbol properties (point, digits, tick value, stops level), always read for that symbol, never from _Symbol. A single OnTick/OnTimer loop calls every instance; an empty symbol name disables the slot. Account-level limits (total open risk, daily loss) sit above the instances and see all of them.
features.rationale: Two separate EAs cannot see each other's exposure; one EA with per-symbol objects gives a single place to cap combined risk. Caveats for honest testing: OnTick fires only for the chart symbol, so the second symbol must be serviced from the timer, and multi-symbol backtests need synchronised history for both symbols. The source EAs are quality 2, so take the structure, not the code.
features.gold_silver_notes: Gold and silver usually move together, so same-direction positions in both are close to one bet and the shared cap must count them jointly. Contract size and tick value differ between the two and between brokers; read them per symbol.

features.name: Metal symbol profile with suffix-tolerant detection
features.description: At OnInit classify the symbol by prefix match (StringFind(sym,"XAUUSD")==0, "GOLD", "XAGUSD", "SILVER") so XAUUSDm or XAGUSD.r still resolve, then load a small profile struct. Keep signal logic shared and volatility-scaled (ATR units); let the profile carry only structural differences: silver gets lower base risk, wider ATR stop multiple, wider trail and more bars between trades. Unrecognised symbols should fail init or require an explicit override.
features.rationale: Exact-name matching silently drops the metal settings on brokers with suffixes, and identical fixed settings mis-size silver. The risk is the opposite extreme: two full hand-tuned parameter tables double the free parameters. Both source EAs are quality 2, so adopt the detection and the idea of a minimal profile, not their numbers.
features.gold_silver_notes: Source values (silver SL 2.0 x ATR vs gold 1.5, base risk 0.3% vs 0.5%) are illustrative only. A prefix-only match misses brokers that put a prefix before the name, so keep a manual symbol-class input as override and log the detected class at start.

features.name: Magic-number namespace per sub-strategy and direction, with permission switches and per-magic statistics
features.description: Derive magics as base + strategy offset (+ direction where needed). Every position lookup, close, modify and history query filters by symbol + magic. Each sub-strategy has open/close permission flags per direction, and counts, lots, floating and closed PnL and last-open time are tracked per magic. An optional mutual lock lets only one sub-strategy hold positions, forced on netting accounts. Manager tools get a scope selector (all/manual/own).
features.rationale: Strict ownership stops the EA from touching manual trades or other EAs, and per-magic statistics let each module be judged and switched off on its own, which is what honest attribution needs. Most common architecture idea in the set, and here popularity matches merit. Magic isolation does not hold on netting accounts (one position per symbol), so the lock must be enforced there.
features.gold_silver_notes: Give each metal its own magic offset so XAUUSD and XAGUSD results never blend. Direction flags allow running one side only without code changes, but that choice should come from out-of-sample evidence, not from the backtest window's trend.

features.name: Duplex: fully separate long-side and short-side parameter sets and timeframes
features.description: Independent parameter block, timeframe, magic number and money management for the long side and the short side, each optimised and enabled separately. If ever used, implement it as two instances of the same signal class with separate configs and magics, default the short config to mirror the long one, and require each side to pass out-of-sample testing on its own.
features.rationale: It doubles the free parameters while halving the trades behind each set, and an optimised long/short asymmetry mostly memorises the drift of the test window. The cheap, useful parts (direction enable flags, separate magics) are already covered by the magic namespace feature.
features.gold_silver_notes: Gold's long drift makes a long-biased duplex look excellent in backtests; that is a bet on the drift continuing, not an edge. Silver would need yet another pair of sets, compounding the problem.

features.name: Fail-fast input validation in OnInit
features.description: OnInit checks every input and cross-input relation (risk > 0, R:R > 0, ATR multiple > 0, stop and breakeven distances > 0, fast period < slow period, symbol recognised) and returns INIT_PARAMETERS_INCORRECT with a printed reason, so the optimiser discards invalid combinations instead of running them. Use INIT_FAILED for resource failures such as an invalid indicator handle, keeping the two cases distinguishable in logs.
features.rationale: A misconfigured EA should never trade, and optimisation results should not contain nonsense passes. It is the cheapest robustness feature in the catalog and has no downside.
features.gold_silver_notes: Extend the checks to the metal's contract: configured stop distance against the symbol's stops level, and the minimum lot against the risk budget, refusing to start rather than rounding risk up on a small account.

features.name: Unified tick-plus-timer cycle: re-entrancy guard, throttle, snapshot, idempotent actions
features.description: OnTick and a 1-second OnTimer both call one Cycle() guarded by a busy flag and server-time throttle. Each cycle builds one snapshot of own positions (symbol + magic, sorted oldest-first: counts, direction, volume-weighted average price, floating PnL) and aborts all actions if it fails. Actions are idempotent: a level counter advances only on a confirmed close; a while loop catches several levels in one gap.
features.rationale: Management keeps running in quiet markets and for the non-chart symbol, repeated passes are harmless, and no rule decides from half-read or inconsistent state. The best evidence comes from the highest-quality sources in the set (79017 q5, 78821 q4). Timer behaviour in the tester depends on the tick model, so confirm that tester and live cycles behave the same.
features.gold_silver_notes: Metals gap over the daily break and on news, so one pass must be able to process several crossed levels. The timer is also what services XAGUSD when the EA sits on an XAUUSD chart.

features.name: Ordered pipeline: exits before entries, one entry gate that never blocks management
features.description: Each cycle runs in a fixed order: refresh rates and buffers (abort if CopyBuffer returns fewer values than requested), then close checks, then stop modifications, then entries, optionally returning after the first action. All entry filters (news, trade-allowed, strategy lock, no re-entry on the bar a series closed) collapse into one CanOpen() gate that guards new entries only; exits and stop management always run.
features.rationale: Reducing risk always takes priority over adding it, and a single gate gives one place to log why no trade was opened. Source 19138 put the gate in front of management as well, which leaves open positions unmanaged exactly when the filter is active; that is the mistake to design out.
features.gold_silver_notes: During news spikes and rollover spread widening, block entries but keep stops managed. A filter that freezes the whole EA abandons a gold position at the worst moment.

features.name: Closed-bar data layer: cached indicator handles and per-timeframe new-bar gates
features.description: Indicator handles are created lazily per symbol/timeframe/parameters, cached in parallel arrays and released in OnDeinit. Values are read from closed bars only (shift >= 1). Each symbol+timeframe has its own new-bar detector (last bar open time), so e.g. H4 structure updates and M15 signal evaluation each run once per closed bar of their own timeframe. Buffers are trimmed to the shortest successful copy.
features.rationale: Closed-bar reads remove intrabar and repainting signals and make coarse tester modes agree with live behaviour. Cached handles avoid leaks and per-tick handle creation, and separate gates per timeframe stop one timeframe's bar event from triggering another's logic.
features.gold_silver_notes: Handles are per symbol, so XAUUSD and XAGUSD never share one. H4 and D1 bar boundaries depend on broker server time, so higher-timeframe structure on gold can differ between brokers; record the server time offset with results.

features.name: Single evaluator for live and replay, with a filter-result bitmask as reason code
features.description: One Checks(direction, shift) function evaluates every entry condition from buffers loaded once into arrays; live trading calls it at shift 1 and any replay or diagnostic calls it at other shifts, so there is no second copy of the rules. Each check result is packed into a bitmask stored with the decision, giving a per-bar reason code for why a trade was or was not taken.
features.rationale: One code path removes the usual drift between live logic and history/visualisation logic, and the bitmask gives honest per-filter attribution. The source also uses the bitmask to rescore every filter combination (EvalCombo); that part is a data-mining tool and should be limited to ablation checks, never to picking the best subset in-sample. Seen in only one EA, but a quality-4 one.
features.gold_silver_notes: Reason codes show per metal how often each filter blocks an entry, which exposes cases where a filter removes most silver trades and leaves too small a sample.

features.name: Trade-validator class for broker constraints, with strict retcode handling
features.description: One class caches symbol constraints (min/max/step volume, stops level, tick size and value, calc mode) with Refresh() and exposes NormalizeVolume, ValidateVolume and ValidateStopLoss, so strategy code never touches raw broker limits; properties are read per position symbol. Order results count as success only for TRADE_RETCODE_DONE, DONE_PARTIAL or NO_CHANGES; anything else is logged and left for the next idempotent cycle.
features.rationale: Most live failures are invalid volumes, invalid stops and misread return codes. Centralising the rules removes scattered assumptions such as a hardcoded pip size, and strict success criteria stop the EA from believing an order went through when it did not.
features.gold_silver_notes: Digits, contract size, tick value, lot step and stops level for gold and silver differ between brokers, so nothing should be hardcoded. Round volume down, not to nearest, so realised risk never exceeds the budget, and refresh constraints before each order.

features.name: Embedded trade-journal export at end of test and session
features.description: Include a journal exporter as a library (#define switch plus #include) and call Export(config, path) from OnDeinit/OnTester so every test and live session writes the same per-trade CSV. Config supports magic lists and ranges ('1001,2000-2999'), symbol wildcards ('XAU*'), common-folder output and UTF-8 BOM. For long live histories, scan deals incrementally in chunks (e.g. 500 per timer call) with a persistent index rather than one blocking pass.
features.rationale: Honest testing needs raw trade records in the same format from the tester and from live trading so the two can be compared outside the terminal's summary report. The chunked incremental scan (75112) is only needed for long live histories and can come later.
features.gold_silver_notes: Wildcards such as 'XAU*' and 'XAG*' keep suffixed symbols in the report. Export and review each metal separately so weak silver results are not hidden behind gold's.

features.name: Unanimous confluence of a few signal modules, with a separate exit module set
features.description: Each enabled module returns long/short/none on the closed bar; an entry needs every enabled module to agree, and opposing votes cancel to zero. A separately configured module set, with its own timeframes, produces the close signal so exits need not mirror entries. Keep to two or three modules with fixed roles and no weights; do not optimise which modules are switched on.
features.rationale: Unanimity adds no weights and the entry/exit decoupling is sound, but each module brings its own parameters and the on/off combination becomes another optimisable dimension. Version 1 is better served by one signal plus the entry gate; add confluence later if a single signal proves too noisy. Sources are quality 2.
features.gold_silver_notes: Requiring many indicators to agree on gold mostly selects strong-trend stretches and shrinks the sample, which makes a backtest look cleaner than it is; check trades per year before trusting it.

features.name: Weighted-score voting with open/close thresholds, or supervisor override by specialist models
features.description: Modules emit 0-100 scores (pattern plus oscillator 80, plain oscillator crossing 40) that are combined and compared with separate open and close thresholds; or a supervisor lets long-only and short-only specialist models override a baseline signal when a gating model agrees. If ever used, fix scores and thresholds a priori and never optimise them together with the underlying indicator parameters.
features.rationale: Scores, weights and two thresholds are correlated free parameters with no physical meaning; an optimiser will find a combination that fits any history, and individual decisions become hard to explain or attribute. The supervisor variant stacks several optimised models on top of each other. The one good idea here, different strength for entry and exit, survives in the unanimous version.
features.gold_silver_notes: Gold alternates between trending and ranging regimes, and tuned weights fit whichever regime dominated the test window. Silver would need its own weights, doubling the fitted surface.

features.name: Veto-only model confirmation layer behind a deterministic pre-filter
features.description: A deterministic closed-bar pre-filter must fire first; only then is a model consulted (rate-limited), and its answer is accepted only if its direction equals the pre-filter and confidence meets a threshold. The model can veto, never originate. Keep it off by default behind a flag. An in-terminal inference library with file-saved weights avoids DLL and web calls, which makes the layer reproducible in the tester.
features.rationale: The veto-only pattern is the safe way to attach any ML or LLM layer, but an external model cannot be reproduced in the Strategy Tester, so its effect cannot be honestly backtested, and a trained network (48097) carries heavy overfitting and maintenance cost. It does not belong in version 1; the base system must stand on its own without it.
features.gold_silver_notes: A model call adds latency on fast gold moves, so it may gate entries only and must never sit in the path of stop management. A model trained on gold should not be assumed to transfer to silver.

features.name: Generic indicator-to-signal adapter table (config-swappable iCustom signals)
features.description: A signal() function maps any iCustom indicator to +1/-1/0 through a type code (zero cross, two-line cross, MA vs close, level cross, slope, non-empty buffer) plus buffer indices, so components are swapped by configuration alone. Acceptable only in a separate research harness; the production EA should compile in one fixed, reviewed signal.
features.rationale: It exists to make indicator shopping cheap, and testing many indicator combinations until one works is the fastest route to a curve-fitted system. It also depends on external indicator binaries whose repainting behaviour the adapter cannot see, and a wrong type code or buffer index fails silently. Source is quality 2.
features.gold_silver_notes: Many custom indicators marketed for gold repaint; plugged in through an adapter they produce backtests that cannot be reproduced live.

features.name: Macro abstraction layer for MT4/MT5 trade calls
features.description: Trade and selection calls (POS_BUY, POS_MODIFY, POS_CLOSE_PARTIAL, POS_SELECT_BY_INDEX and similar) are defined per platform under #ifdef so one logic body compiles for both MQL4 and MQL5. For a new bot, target MQL5 only and put the trade calls behind your own executor class instead of macros.
features.rationale: Dual-platform support doubles the test surface and hides real differences in the order/position model and in tester fidelity behind macros that are hard to debug. A new MQL5-only bot gains nothing from it; the useful part, one abstraction over raw trade calls, is already delivered by the executor and validator classes.
features.gold_silver_notes: A combined gold and silver bot relies on MT5's multi-symbol testing; keeping MT4 compatibility would constrain the design to what the older tester can verify.

features.name: Cross-terminal state sharing through a FILE_COMMON CSV
features.description: Terminals on one machine exchange state through a CSV in the shared common data folder (FileOpen with FILE_COMMON, polled from OnTimer), needing no DLL or network. It can publish a cross-account exposure figure or a risk-lock flag. Include a timestamp in the file and treat stale, missing or unreadable data as locked, so a failure blocks new entries rather than allowing them.
features.rationale: Only needed when the bot runs on more than one terminal or account. It adds a failure mode (stale or locked file) and cannot be exercised meaningfully in the tester, so it stays behind a flag with a fail-safe default. Source is a quality-2 copier; take the transport idea only.
features.gold_silver_notes: Useful if gold and silver are traded on different accounts or brokers and combined metal exposure must still be capped. With both in one EA, the shared account-level risk layer already covers it.

common_mistakes: Putting the news/trade-allowed gate in front of the whole OnTick, so stop and exit management also stop while the filter is active (19138). The gate must guard new entries only.
Matching the symbol by exact name, so broker suffixes (XAUUSDm, XAGUSD.r) silently fall back to default, non-metal settings; prefix-only matching still misses brokers that add a leading prefix.
Shipping two full hand-tuned parameter tables for gold and silver as 'presets' (both source EAs are quality 2), which doubles free parameters instead of scaling one logic by volatility.
Optimising the long side and the short side separately (duplex), which fits the trend of the test window and halves the sample behind each parameter set.
Combining signals through weighted scores, thresholds or stacked supervisor models: many correlated free parameters with no physical meaning and no way to attribute a decision.
Making signals swappable by configuration (generic iCustom adapter), which turns the EA into an indicator-shopping tool and hides repainting inputs.
Letting the EA run with invalid or inconsistent inputs instead of failing OnInit, or returning INIT_FAILED where INIT_PARAMETERS_INCORRECT would let the optimiser skip the pass.
Acting on partial data: continuing when CopyBuffer returns fewer values than requested, or when the position snapshot failed part-way through.
Treating any non-error order result as success; only DONE, DONE_PARTIAL and NO_CHANGES should count.
Rescanning positions separately inside each rule, so different rules see different state within the same tick, instead of reading one snapshot per cycle.
Driving everything from OnTick only, so management stalls in quiet markets and for symbols other than the chart symbol.
Non-idempotent management: advancing a partial-close or level counter before the close is confirmed, or handling only one level per pass so a gap through several levels is missed.
Using _Symbol/_Point/_Digits for every position in a multi-symbol EA instead of reading properties for each position's own symbol.
Sharing one magic number across sub-strategies or directions, so closes and statistics interfere; and assuming magic isolation works on netting accounts, where there is only one position per symbol.
Using one new-bar flag for all timeframes, or evaluating signals on the forming bar instead of the closed bar.
Keeping separate code for live decisions and for history/replay, which drifts apart so the backtest no longer tests what trades live.
Using a filter-combination rescoring tool to pick the best in-sample subset of filters rather than for diagnostics.
Letting an external model originate trades, calling it on every tick, or relying on a layer that cannot run in the Strategy Tester and therefore cannot be honestly backtested.
Forcing exits to mirror entry logic instead of giving exits their own independently configured conditions.
Re-entering on the same bar on which a trade series was just closed.
Creating indicator handles on every call or never releasing them, instead of caching per symbol and releasing in OnDeinit.
Scanning the whole deal history in one blocking pass on the terminal thread.
Carrying MT4/MT5 compatibility macros into a new MQL5-only bot, doubling the test surface for no benefit.
Copying architecture from low-quality EAs wholesale: more than half of these ideas come from quality 2-3 code, where the pattern is worth keeping but the implementation and numbers are not.

Reading bar-0 (forming bar) indicator or price values for signals, so the signal repaints within the bar and differs between tester modes; several raw ideas carry the reader's note 'would need shifting to closed bars' (21511, 8544, 8246, 17184, 13625, 68125).
Triggering on a tick pierce of a range or level instead of a closed-bar close beyond it, which buys wick fakeouts.

Thresholds in fixed points/pips (range width, breakout buffer, minimum gap, minimum distance from MA, oscillator-volume thresholds) instead of ATR/ADR/spread units; they do not transfer between XAUUSD and XAGUSD or across volatility regimes.

Session windows defined in raw server hours with no GMT-offset or DST handling, so the 'Asian range' drifts by broker and season; weekend and short Sunday bars counted into N-candle windows or producing trivially narrow ranges.
Building the session range from chart-timeframe bars, making the range depend on which chart the EA is attached to, instead of from M1 data.
New-bar detection with one static timestamp shared across symbols/timeframes, marking the bar consumed before filters run, or silently losing the bar's signal when CopyBuffer fails.
Latches and 'already traded' flags kept only in static variables, so a restart re-enters the same level, bar or expansion; no rebuild of range/setup state from history on init.
Levels and zones reused indefinitely: no single-use flag, no expiry, no invalidation after a true close-through, so stale levels trade days later.

Pending-order hygiene gaps: no OCO (opposite leg left alive after a fill), same-side pendings stacked instead of replaced, expiry handled only by the EA while online instead of broker-side, no handling of a failed delete.

Ignoring spread in stop-order prices and in reward-to-risk (bid-based levels for buy stops), and ignoring stops/freeze levels, leading to rejected orders or trades that cannot pay after costs; 'fixing' an infeasible entry by pushing it out and shifting the target.
Re-pegging pending orders every tick or bar without a throttle, generating modify spam and rejections right before news.
Fading the first touch of an oscillator or band extreme, and attaching oscillator entries to grid, martingale or recovery position management where averaging hides how weak the trigger is.
Weighted confluence scores with arbitrary constants (50 plus/minus points, 0.3/0.3/0.2/0.2, 40/30/30) that cannot be ablated and whose components are correlated.
Presenting in-EA re-optimisation, virtual-trade pattern tables or perceptron votes as 'adaptive' with no out-of-sample validation, no minimum sample count and state that depends on EA start time.
Treating tick volume as real volume in impulse, session-open and Force-Index style filters; on metals CFDs it is broker-specific quote count and differs between history and live.
Stacking many filters and separately tuned parameter sets (per-direction SL/TP, second oscillator, adaptive thresholds, extra MA confirmations), each adding a fitting knob without evidence it helps.
Immediate stop-and-reverse on the same tick, or opening the reverse position without confirming the close succeeded; implementation in the source (10848) was noted as unreliable.
Entering late into a move already in progress: placing breakout orders after the forming bar has already broken the range, or taking an expansion already underway after a restart.
Running opposite logics on the same levels (breakout and sweep/fade, or trend-inside and fade-outside envelope maps) without deciding which module owns the level, risking contradictory positions.
Relying on manually drawn chart lines or discretionary levels for entries, which cannot be backtested or reproduced.

features.name: Closed-bar-only signal evaluation with new-bar gate
features.rationale: The most widely shared sound practice in this category (about 52 of the cited EAs read shifts 1/2). It makes every-tick, 1-minute-OHLC and live runs produce the same signals, removes repaint, and adds no tunable parameter. The recount flag (20943) and filter-before-consume ordering (62732) close the two usual holes. Bound the retry to a short period after bar open so the entry price cannot drift far from the signal close.

features.name: Session/opening range builder from M1 bars
features.rationale: The higher-quality gold breakout EAs in the sample (75586, 76153, 78688, 78293, 17465) are all built on a session range, and the builder is the part that most often goes wrong: chart-timeframe dependence, raw server hours, weekend bars, state lost on restart. Building from M1 with explicit time conversion and a history rebuild gives a range that is reproducible in the tester and live. Window times are the only parameters; keep them coarse and do not optimise them finely.

features.name: Closed-bar range breakout with buffer and entry window
features.rationale: Closed-bar acceptance beyond the range is the simplest trigger in the sample that is fully reproducible in the tester (market order at the next bar open, no dependence on intrabar fill modelling), and it filters wick fakeouts. Parameters are few: buffer and window length. The cost is a later entry and a larger stop distance than a stop order, but that cost is visible in the test instead of hidden. The whole-bar-outside variant (18704, 7612) is stricter but comes from lower-quality EAs; keep it as an option only.

features.name: Range-width and compression gate
features.rationale: Stops and position size are usually derived from the range, so a degenerate range damages risk directly: too narrow puts the stop inside spread/noise and inflates the lot under fixed-risk sizing; too wide gives poor reward-to-risk. A two-bound gate in ADR/ATR units (17465 uses 23.6%-76.4% of ADR) is cheap and defensible. Keep the bounds wide and few. The NR-N, squeeze-latch and rising-but-capped-volatility variants add lookback parameters and belong behind a flag.

features.name: Higher-timeframe trend-side filter on closed bars
features.rationale: Present in about 18 EAs, including q5 77691 and q4 78968 (close on the EMA200 side). One closed-bar trend state removes counter-trend breakouts at low cost. The risk is that every extra filter or tuned period is a fitting knob, so ship exactly one, with a switch, and report results with and without it. SuperTrend, SilverTrend and ADX forms are interchangeable alternatives, not additions; rank-correlation (J_TPO) and Volatility Quality variants add complexity with no supporting evidence here.

features.name: Setup lifecycle state machine with single-use latches
features.rationale: Duplicate and stale entries are a survival issue, not an optimisation: without latches a level retriggers after a stop-out and a restart re-enters. About 17 EAs carry some form (swept flag, consumed fractal, per-bar level latch, squeeze re-arm, per-direction latch), and the q5/q4 sweep EAs add confirmation windows with expiry. No edge parameters apart from expiry length. Prefer state derived from broker records (8417, 63916) over static variables, which several lower-quality EAs rely on.

features.name: Pre-trade feasibility and net-RR gate with logged reject reasons
features.rationale: Hard feasibility checks protect the account from trades that cannot pay after costs and from order rejections, and they make every non-trade explainable. One parameter (minimum net RR) plus a spread cap. Drawn from 75652 (net RR and logged reasons), 8594/21452/71521 (stops-level checks) and 78688 (spread compensation). Prefer skipping an infeasible setup to pushing the entry out and shifting the target as 71521 does, which silently changes the strategy being tested.

features.name: Two-sided pending stop bracket with broker-side expiry and OCO
features.rationale: Well engineered in the best sources (75586, 78688, 73711, 11350, 78308): broker-side expiry survives a disconnected terminal and OCO removes the whipsaw second leg. Kept behind a flag because a stop at the range edge fills on the first tick through the level, where slippage is worst and false breaks most common, and the tester fills it more kindly than a live server. If enabled, every hygiene rule is mandatory. About six news-timed straddles reuse the same OCO/expiry logic; those are counted under the price-chasing pendings feature.

features.name: Liquidity sweep-and-reclaim (failed breakout) entry
features.rationale: The best-specified reversal entry in the sample: 77639 (q5) and 77094 (q4) implement it fully on closed bars with ATR-qualified wicks, confirmation windows and single-use levels. It is a second strategy with its own parameters (pivot width, wick multiple, confirmation bars, minimum range), so it should follow the breakout engine and be tested separately, not blended into it. Manually drawn levels (14206) cannot be backtested and touch-count clustering (71645) adds tuning; neither is needed.

features.name: Fresh closed-bar trend trigger: N-bar channel breakout or MA cross
features.rationale: Simple and low-parameter. 77691 (q5, gold H4) shows the right channel form with a freshness test and no bar-0 data; 78968 (q4) shows the right MA form. Optional because v1 should carry one entry engine, and MA crosses lag and whipsaw on intraday gold. Useful as a transparent benchmark for the session engine. Adaptive averages (913), band-cross confirmations (48251/45323) and minimum-distance/slope/volume add-ons (62684) add parameters without evidence of benefit in these sources.

features.name: Scale-free candle-quality metrics as confirmation
features.rationale: Ratio definitions (268, 324, 78343, 13901) are scale-free and transfer across instruments, and a single confirmation such as 'confirmation bar range above 0.3 ATR' is used by the better sweep EAs. But every added candle condition is another threshold, and pattern catalogues (three inside, morning star, engulfing) are not an edge on their own, as the readers noted. Allow at most one such gate per entry type, default off, justified by ablation. The tick-volume terms are the weakest part.

features.name: Fair value gap / order-block zone retest
features.rationale: A closed-bar pullback entry with a registry, one-trade-per-zone flag and invalidation is implementable, but the dedicated sources are q2-q3, definitions vary between authors (gap size, tolerance, what counts as an order block, zone expiry), and requiring OB and FVG overlap (79285) multiplies the free choices. High curve-fitting risk. Consider only after the core engine is validated, with an ATR-scaled minimum gap and invalidation on closed bars (68125 evaluates it intrabar).

features.name: Cross-symbol directional proxy
features.rationale: Supported by only three low-value ideas plus a 'macro proxy' term inside 75652's score, and the gold applications were suggested by the readers, not implemented in the sources. It adds data dependencies (several symbols, synchronised history, broker-specific symbol names) and multi-symbol tester complexity for an unproven filter. Defer. If tried, log it first as a diagnostic and promote it to a veto only if it helps out of sample.

features.name: Oscillator zone-exit / band re-entry reversal trigger
features.rationale: Popular (about 22 EAs), but many hosts are grid, martingale or recovery systems (79021, 76605, 72278, 71700, 21511) where averaging down, not the trigger, produces the equity curve. As a standalone entry it fades moves in an instrument that trends hard, and it carries many thresholds (period, levels, adaptive steps, second oscillator, lookback memory) that fit easily. Not for v1 as a trigger. The zone-exit idea survives only as a possible pullback timer in the trend direction, later and behind a flag.

features.name: Weighted additive confluence score gate
features.rationale: Scores make weak evidence look like confirmation. Points and weights (50 plus/minus n, 0.3/0.3/0.2/0.2, 40/30/30) are arbitrary free parameters, the components are correlated, and a threshold on the sum cannot be ablated, so nobody can tell which condition earns its place. This is the most direct route to a fitted backtest in this category. Keep only what is honest in the sources: per-signal reason logging and the separate net-RR check, both carried by the feasibility gate.

features.name: Price-chasing and stacked pending orders (news straddles, trailing stop-entries, stop ladders)
features.rationale: Three variants of one weakness: the fill cannot be modelled or the exposure stacks. News straddles (7 EAs, all q2-q3) depend on fills during the widest spreads and largest gaps of the day, which the tester cannot reproduce, and re-pegging creates modify traffic and rejections. Trailing stop-entries (919, 11449) enter on a fixed-size bounce that a closed-bar reclaim confirms more honestly. Stop ladders, especially two-sided ones (26718), are grids by another name and multiply correlated risk at extremes; a one-sided add-on with a total-risk cap is the only form worth revisiting much later.

features.name: Self-optimising and learned signal generators
features.rationale: Adaptivity inside the EA is in-sample optimisation running continuously: it picks whatever worked over the last N bars with no out-of-sample check, carries hidden state that differs between tester and live starts, and makes results unreproducible. Sources are mostly q1-q3, and the readers themselves attach conditions (out-of-sample validation, minimum trade count) that the code does not meet. Per-direction parameter sets (8499) double the fitted inputs. Triple-barrier labelling (1229) is sound but belongs in offline research.

features.name: Tick-driven triggers: z-score bursts, renko bricks, intrabar displacement
features.rationale: Tick-window statistics depend on the broker's tick feed, on latency and on the tester's tick model; the same EA sees different tick counts live and in history, so results are not honestly testable. The self-calibrating z-score (77167, 77220, both q4) is well built and volatility-adaptive and the per-bar latch (244) is sound, but short-horizon edges are consumed by metals spreads. Out of scope for a survival-first v1; revisit only with real-tick tests and measured live slippage.

common_mistakes: Fixed point or pip distances for SL, TP, breakeven, trail and profit tiers (20/35/50 pips, 7.7 pips, 5-point steps) instead of ATR, R or structure units; they break across brokers' digit conventions for gold and silver and across volatility regimes. Readers repeatedly flagged 'would need ATR units'.
Deriving 'pip' size from hard-coded digits instead of symbol properties (point, tick size, tick value).
Trailing on every tick with no minimum-improvement step or rate limit, producing modify spam and 'too many requests' rejections on fast metals ticks.
Sending SL/TP modifications without checking stops level and freeze level (checking only the side of price, or nothing), and retrying failed modifies with no cap.
Management routines that can widen risk: a mode switch that re-stamps wider SL/TP on open positions, a take-profit pulled toward price or pushed outward after entry, trails that are not ratchet-only.
Hidden or virtual stops used as the only stop, with no broker-side hard SL behind them.
Breakeven set at the exact entry price with no offset for spread, commission and swap, so 'breakeven' is a net loss.
Breakeven and trailing written as independent routines that fight over the SL, or a trail that starts before breakeven or while the trade is still negative and so tightens the initial stop.
Using a stale local SL value after a successful modify in the same tick, and not handling SL == 0 (especially on the sell side, where 'new SL below old SL' can never be true for zero).
Reading ATR or other indicator values from the forming bar (shift 0), so the trail distance changes inside the bar and tester and live behaviour diverge.

Partial closes computed as a percentage of the remaining volume instead of the original, without lot-step normalisation, leaving dust below minimum lot, or without a once-only flag so a stage fires repeatedly.
Keeping exit state (partial stage, peak profit, initial volume, entry timeframe) only in memory so it is lost on restart, never pruning ticket lists, or relying solely on order comments.
Time stops measured in wall-clock hours that count weekends and market closures as holding time.
Polling a close hour every tick and re-sending close requests, or all-or-nothing basket close loops without a retry latch and without iterating backwards.
Relying on broker-side pending-order expiry, leaving the surviving leg of a straddle alive, or letting stale pendings trigger after the volatility regime has changed.
Assuming the entry order always carries its SL/TP (not true on market-execution brokers) with no check for naked positions.
Managing positions without a symbol + magic ownership filter, or stamping the manager's magic onto positions it does not own.
Close-and-reverse without verifying that the close succeeded, leaving unintended hedged or doubled exposure.
Basket money targets on raw floating profit that exclude swap and commission and do not scale with lots, used as the only exit for grid or martingale baskets that have no per-position or basket stop.
SL and TP derived from unrelated measures (band width for SL, ATR for TP), hard TP caps, or stops so wide (10x ATR) that they are decorative, making risk:reward accidental.
Parameter proliferation exposed to the optimiser: seven selectable trail methods, per-signal and per-timeframe SL/TP tables, multi-tier ladders, two-speed and volatility-interpolated trail widths.
Money-denominated trails and targets that ignore volatility and mean different things per symbol and lot size.
Judging exit logic by win rate (partials, tight breakeven) rather than net R after costs, and trusting tick-level breakeven or trail results from a tester that fills stops with zero slippage.

features.name: Initial protective stop from structure or ATR, clamped and broker-valid
features.rationale: Defines 1R, which the position sizer and every later exit stage depend on. Structure and ATR stops scale across volatility regimes and brokers; fixed-point stops do not. One or two parameters, so it is hard to curve-fit. Do not copy the per-signal or per-timeframe SL tables (7917, 17137) or the 10x-ATR stop with a hard cap (22705): they multiply fitted parameters or make the stop decorative.

features.name: Take-profit as an R-multiple of the stop distance (or a structural target)
features.rationale: A single RR input is transparent, testable and consistent with risk-based sizing. Structural targets with a minimum-room filter are a reasonable later variant. Avoid SL and TP taken from unrelated volatility measures (63916 notes the ratio must be re-tuned), forecast-derived or statistical targets (48097, 8397) and timeframe-keyed TP tables (12208): they add fitted parameters without supporting evidence.

features.name: Single SL modification gateway: tighten-only, broker-valid, step-gated, throttled
features.rationale: The most widely repeated and least controversial mechanism in the set. It makes every management routine idempotent and risk-reducing by construction, prevents invalid-stops rejections and modify spam, and has almost no tunable surface. It also blocks bugs seen elsewhere, such as a mode switch that re-stamps wider SL/TP on open positions (79181) or two routines modifying in one tick with a stale SL value.

features.name: Staged exit pipeline with fixed precedence and profit-only trail activation
features.rationale: This is architecture, not a tunable edge. It removes ordering bugs (trail acting before breakeven, routines overwriting each other) and makes behaviour deterministic and testable. The monotonic-candidate form (62732) needs no stored state, so it survives restarts. Many EAs reach the same result with flags ('trail only after breakeven', 'profit-only trailing'); the max() formulation is the cleanest version.

features.name: Breakeven with net-of-cost lock offset
features.rationale: Present in about 30 EAs, but popularity is not merit. The trigger distance is one of the most curve-fitted exit inputs, and a tight breakeven converts winners into scratch trades while flattering win rate. A profit-only ATR trail crosses entry on its own. Ship behind a flag (default off), trigger in R, and enable only if out-of-sample tests show lower drawdown without destroying expectancy.

features.name: Closed-bar ATR (chandelier) trailing stop
features.rationale: The best-supported trailing form, including the highest-quality gold EA in the sample (77691). One or two parameters, volatility-adaptive, monotonic, and when evaluated on bar close it is insensitive to tick-model quality, which keeps backtests honest. Best price since entry can be recomputed from bars since POSITION_TIME, so no persisted state is needed. Keep a disable flag so plain SL/TP is testable as a baseline; adaptive-width variants stay out of v1.

features.name: Structure-based trail (Donchian or swing) behind a pluggable candidate-SL interface
features.rationale: Structure trails tolerate pullbacks better than a fixed distance and suit breakout or trend systems, but swing detection adds parameters (N, fractal width, timeframe, offset). The pluggable interface is good engineering; exposing seven methods (SAR, MA, fractal, percent of profit and so on) as optimisable inputs is a curve-fitting menu. Ship the ATR chandelier in v1 and add a Donchian channel as the single alternative later.

features.name: Scale-out ladder in R-multiples of original volume
features.rationale: Smooths the equity curve and appears in several of the better EAs, but it adds four to six parameters (levels and fractions), needs persistent per-position state, and typically raises win rate while lowering expectancy versus one clean exit. It is impossible at minimum lot. Add it only after v1 is validated with a single exit, and judge it on net R after costs, not on win rate.

features.name: Restart-safe per-position exit state and strict ownership
features.rationale: Without it a terminal restart, VPS reboot or recompile silently changes exit behaviour (repeated partials, lost 1R reference, forgotten time stop) and live results diverge from the backtest. Cheap when designed in from the start and painful to retrofit. Stateless derivations (10984: SL-versus-entry as the breakeven flag) are the most robust form and should be preferred wherever possible.

features.name: Time stop in traded bars, optionally conditional on progress
features.rationale: Bounds exposure time, swap cost and the chance of carrying a dead trade into an unrelated event. One parameter, stateless (open time lives on the position), restart-safe and easy to verify in the tester. Ship the simple unconditional form in v1; the conditional variants (71521, 73711) add a second parameter and belong behind a flag.

features.name: Session-end / end-of-day flatten and stale-position cleanup
features.rationale: Removes rollover spread blow-outs, swap and overnight gap risk for strategies that were only validated intraday. A single clock parameter, deterministic and easy to check in the tester. Seen in few EAs, but it is one of the cheapest survival mechanisms. A swing mode may disable it explicitly; the default should be flat at the cut-off.

features.name: Pending-order hygiene: bar-count expiry and OCO cancellation
features.rationale: Needed only if entries use stop or limit orders, but then it is mandatory: a stale breakout level triggers in a different volatility regime, and an uncancelled opposite leg creates an unplanned second position. Simple, deterministic, one parameter, and independent of which expiration modes the broker supports.

features.name: Auto-attach missing protective stop (naked-position safety net)
features.rationale: Enforces the invariant 'no position without a broker-side stop', the bot's main survival property. Covers market-execution brokers that refuse SL in the entry request, failed modifies and manual interference. It has no tunable edge, so there is nothing to overfit. Restrict it to owned positions; attaching stops to every position on the account (61119) is a manager tool, not bot behaviour.

features.name: Virtual / stealth SL-TP levels hidden from the broker
features.rationale: A stealth-only stop vanishes when the terminal, VPS or connection fails, and it fills at market after the cross. The tester fills it optimistically, so results cannot be verified honestly, and several source EAs (17184) have no hard stop behind it at all. The readers consistently rate it useful only as an inner layer inside a hard stop; even that form should wait until after v1.

features.name: Basket / aggregate exits (net breakeven, money target, basket trail, pairwise unwind)
features.rationale: It exists to manage grid, martingale and averaging baskets, which hide risk behind a high win rate and have open-ended loss unless a basket stop exists. Money targets are not tied to market structure and are trivially curve-fitted. A one-position-per-symbol bot has no use for it. Keep only the reusable hygiene: P/L net of swap and commission, and close-all with a retry latch.

features.name: Secondary profit-lock ratchets, adaptive tightening and post-entry TP changes
features.rationale: Each is individually reasonable, but every one adds two or more thresholds and overlaps with the ATR trail; stacking them is a classic way to fit a backtest. Do not use the money-denominated versions (63569, 76605), fixed-pip tiers (17184, 8246) or TP manipulation (19963, 12208, 69651). If one is wanted later, choose a single ratchet in R and compare it out of sample against the plain chandelier.

features.name: Signal-driven exits and verified close-then-reverse
features.rationale: The verified close-then-open pattern (23220) and separate close permissions giving an exit-only mode (20885) are sound engineering and should be used wherever the strategy reverses. Indicator-specific exit rules (CCI extreme 12872, MA ladder 10848, profit-sign filter 25848) are strategy content with extra fitted parameters; they should arrive only with the strategy that justifies them, and always inside the hard SL.

features.name: Pyramiding into profit with capped adds
features.rationale: Supported by a single EA (17065), whose reader noted it needs an ATR step and stop-to-breakeven to be robust. Adds raise the average entry, so a normal pullback after the last add erases open profit, and step and cap are easy to fit. Not for v1; consider only after the single-position system shows an out-of-sample edge, with aggregated risk accounting.

common_mistakes: Using SYMBOL_POINT (or a hard-coded pip value) where SYMBOL_TRADE_TICK_SIZE is required, so loss per lot is wrong on metals where tick size and point differ (149, 11472, 40252, 19392, 24786, 22705, 46309).
Trusting SYMBOL_TRADE_TICK_VALUE without a cross-check; it is reported wrong for XAUUSD on some brokers and on non-USD accounts, and the generic value is used instead of TICK_VALUE_LOSS.
Raising a too-small lot to SYMBOL_VOLUME_MIN (clamp to min) instead of skipping, which silently exceeds the risk budget on small accounts, most severely on silver.
Rounding lots to the nearest step instead of flooring, hard-coding two lot decimals, or flooring without an epsilon so floating-point error drops a whole step.
Falling back to a fixed lot (or 0.01) when tick value, tick size or the stop distance is zero, instead of refusing the trade (74840, 71120, 71583, 28117).
Sizing from one stop distance and placing another: lot computed before the stop is widened to the broker stops level, or from fixed points while an ATR stop is actually sent.
Allowing percent-risk sizing with the stop loss disabled, or accepting contradictory inputs (both fixed lot and risk) without failing at init.
Using free margin as the risk base, so position size changes with whatever else is open rather than with capital.
Using margin (free margin / margin per lot) as the sizing method instead of only as a ceiling on a stop-based lot.
No margin check before sending, a buffer so thin (98%) it gives no protection, or stepping the lot down one step at a time in a loop instead of computing the affordable lot directly.
Ignoring pending orders when computing exposure and margin, and ignoring SYMBOL_VOLUME_LIMIT and ACCOUNT_LIMIT_ORDERS, so stacked pendings can all trigger into more exposure than intended.
No absolute ceiling: unbounded risk-percent input, no max lot, no max risk money, so a tiny stop distance or bad symbol data yields a huge lot.
Min-lot fallback with a generous second cap (5%) that makes the headline risk percent misleading, with no log of how often it was used.
Daily loss limits checked only after the loss, so the trade that breaches the limit is always permitted; the next trade is not sized against the remaining allowance.

Keeping loss-streak and entries-per-day counters only in memory (OnTrade counters) so they reset on restart, counting deals instead of closed positions, or counting by symbol without the magic number.

Increasing risk after wins, scaling by signal score or Kelly, or multiplying lots after losses; stacking many adaptive multipliers (streak, win rate, drawdown, regime, hour of day) until the sizing cannot be tested.
Fixed-point stops and targets that do not scale with gold's price level or volatility over a multi-year test, and arbitrary Fibonacci constants treated as if they were tested values.
Reading ATR or range from the still-forming bar rather than closed bars, and using true range on intraday metals bars where the session-break gap inflates the unit.
Not verifying the final rounded lot's real loss and margin before sending, and duplicating the same check at several call sites with slightly different logic.
Treating XAUUSD and XAGUSD risk budgets as independent although both are USD-quoted metals that usually move together.

features.name: Loss-at-stop sizing via OrderCalcProfit
features.rationale: The only sizing method in the set that does not depend on the EA author's own contract-size, tick-value or currency-conversion arithmetic. All five quality-5 EAs that size by risk use it. It defines the money lost at the stop, which is what makes every other risk limit and every backtest statistic (R multiples, % drawdown) meaningful. The verification pass after rounding (79017) is cheap and catches rounding or data errors.

features.name: Tick-value / tick-size risk formula (fallback only)
features.rationale: By far the most common method (about a third of all risk ideas), and correct when the broker's tick value is right, but it trusts a field that is known to be unreliable on metals. Keep it only behind OrderCalcProfit, as 78293 does; a v1 can equally just skip the trade when OrderCalcProfit fails. Hand-rolled conversion through a located FX pair (71657) and measuring tick value from an open position's profit (71700) are workarounds for the same weakness and add code that is hard to test.

features.name: Never-round-up lot normalisation (skip below minimum)
features.rationale: Rounding can only be allowed to reduce risk. Raising to the minimum lot is the most common way a stated risk percent becomes false on a small account, and it is invisible in a backtest report. Skipping with a logged reason keeps the test honest: the report then shows the account is too small for the strategy instead of hiding it. The epsilon (79234) and step-derived digits (1397, 78343, 78308) prevent invalid-volume rejections.

features.name: Guarded minimum-lot fallback with a second risk cap
features.rationale: A controlled exception to the skip rule that lets a small account trade at all, with the excess risk bounded and visible. It is honest only if the second cap is tight and every use is reported; 78259 uses 1.5%, while 75652 allows 5%, which makes the headline risk percent misleading. Behind a flag, off by default.

features.name: Margin affordability pre-check with free-margin buffer
features.rationale: Prevents 'not enough money' rejections and keeps a reserve of free margin so an adverse move does not immediately approach stop-out. Seen in 19 EAs with buffers from 80% to 98%; the tighter buffers (98% in a martingale EA) defeat the purpose. Computing the affordable lot directly is better than stepping down one volume step at a time (63193). Do the check in one place, not duplicated at call sites.

features.name: Aggregate exposure caps (total lots, positions, volume limit, pending reserve)
features.rationale: Per-trade risk says nothing about total risk when several positions or pending orders are open. A simple cap on positions and total lots is cheap and bounds the worst case; the broker limits (volume limit, order count) avoid rejections. The pending-order margin reserve (78308) matters only for strategies that place stop or limit orders and can stay off otherwise. Compute from positions and orders, not from in-memory counters.

features.name: Hard ceilings: max lot, max risk money, bounded risk percent
features.rationale: A last line of defence against a sizing bug, a bad tick value, a near-zero stop distance or a mistyped input. The absolute money cap (59001, 71521) also keeps long compounding backtests from producing unrealistic lot sizes that the market could not fill. Costs a few lines and has no tunable effect on the edge.

features.name: Lot cap from remaining daily loss budget
features.rationale: Seen in only one EA, but it closes a real hole: most daily loss limits are checked after the loss has happened, so the trade that breaks the limit is always allowed. Sizing the next trade against what is left makes the daily limit a planned bound rather than a reaction. Requires a daily loss limit and a clearly defined day boundary to exist.

features.name: Single pre-trade gate with logged reasons and per-day entry limits
features.rationale: Puts every refusal in one audited place and makes each skipped trade explainable in the log, which is what makes a test honestly reviewable. The per-direction daily latch (7612) and entries-per-day cap bound the damage from repeated re-entry after a failed signal. The thresholds themselves (max spread, session, entries per day) are parameters, so keep them few and do not optimise them finely.

features.name: Init-time validation of the sizing configuration
features.rationale: An undefined-risk configuration should not be able to start, either live or as one pass of an optimisation. Rejecting it at init removes whole classes of meaningless optimiser results (for example percent risk with no stop) and gives the user a clear message instead of rejected orders later.

features.name: Loss-streak risk throttle (reduction only)
features.rationale: Anti-martingale reduction can only lower exposure, so it is safe in the survival sense, and seven EAs carry some form of it. But it helps only if losses cluster, which must be shown rather than assumed, and its thresholds are easy to fit to one backtest's drawdown. The stacked version in 71521 (streak, win rate, drawdown, regime, hour-of-day P/L) is too many knobs to test honestly; the rolling loss-rate version in 8594 is a cleaner alternative. Keep behind a flag.

features.name: Volatility-unit stop distance (ATR or gap-free mean range)
features.rationale: A stop expressed in a volatility unit adapts to regime and price level with two parameters, and combined with loss-at-stop sizing it gives the same money risk on every trade. That is the minimum needed for a strategy tested over many years of changing gold volatility. The unit must come from closed bars and the lot must be sized from the stop actually placed (79181 makes this explicit). The KVR variant in 74840 is interesting but is an extra layer to fit.

features.name: Structural stop clamped to a volatility band, target as R multiple
features.rationale: Only applies to strategies that have a structure to anchor to (breakout box, swing). The valuable part is the band: it stops a tiny structure from producing a tight stop and oversized lot, and a huge one from producing an untradeably wide stop. The specific constants in the sources (0.618, 1.382, 1.618, 61.8%) are arbitrary Fibonacci numbers; use round values and do not optimise them. Whether to clamp or reject is a design choice that changes the trade set, so test both.

features.name: Percent-of-price stop and target distances
features.rationale: Solves the price-level problem of fixed-point stops with one parameter and no indicator, which makes it easy to test honestly. It does not adapt to volatility regime, so it is weaker than a volatility unit as the primary stop. Most useful as a sanity bound on the volatility stop or as a baseline to compare against.

features.name: Broker stops-level and freeze-level floor applied before sizing
features.rationale: Avoids invalid-stops rejections, and the ordering matters: if the stop is widened after the lot was computed, the trade carries more risk than budgeted. 78778 widens first and then sizes; several others bump the stop at send time. A skip option is safer than widening when the required distance is far from the strategy's intended stop.

features.name: Selectable risk base: fixed money, balance or equity; per-symbol virtual equity
features.rationale: What the risk percent is a percent of changes both live behaviour and how a backtest reads. Fixed-money risk (78891, 71583, 72527) removes compounding so the equity curve and drawdown reflect the edge, not the sizing; percent mode is then a separate, explicit choice. Free margin as a base (149, 11472, and a mode in the 21361 family) shrinks and grows with open positions and is not a measure of capital. Virtual equity (611) is useful later but adds state to maintain.

features.name: Scaling size up by signal confidence, Kelly or win streaks
features.rationale: Variable sizing by score or recent results multiplies the degrees of freedom of the system and lets a backtest improve by concentrating size on trades that happened to win. Kelly from a small recent sample is extremely noisy and overstates the edge. The sources themselves mark the increase side as not advised (63193, 71521). Flat risk per trade keeps the test interpretable: every trade counts equally.

features.name: Lot sizing not tied to the stop (balance steps, drawdown budget, margin fraction, lot multiplication)
features.rationale: These schemes hide risk: the same lot is used whether the stop is near or far, so loss per trade varies with volatility and the stated 'risk' input means something else. The drawdown-budget version (913) hard-wires a backtest's maximum drawdown into live sizing, which is curve fitting by construction. Lot multiplication after losses is martingale; a cap on the number of multiplications (21511) limits it but does not make it safe.

common_mistakes: Keeping the day-start reference, equity peak, trade counters and lock flags only in memory, so a restart, recompile or VPS move resets the baseline and grants a fresh loss budget (flagged as 'needs persistence' on 72527, 76153, 71467, 77167, 79285, 8594, 78293, 61319).
Measuring the daily loss on balance or realised P/L only, ignoring floating loss (77167, 77220, 56126), so the lock fires after the damage is already open.
Leaving swap, commission and fees out of P/L sums, or matching deals by date without HistorySelect (56126), which understates losses.
Counting deposits, withdrawals and broker credit as trading result or as equity, which moves the floor in the wrong direction.
Triggering exactly at the limit with no buffer for slippage, spread and gaps during liquidation, so the real limit is breached while closing.
Computing a breach flag but never enforcing it, or leaving the wiring incomplete or broken (56126, 9499, 12641 trailing lock).
One-shot close-all with no latch or retry, no deletion of pending orders, and no entry lock afterwards, so failed closes linger and the EA re-enters immediately.
Flattening or modifying every position on the account without a magic/symbol filter (61319, 61119, 8366, 22001), interfering with manual trades and other EAs.
Auto-releasing a drawdown lock when equity partly recovers (71583), or implementing the halt by simulating keystrokes (14773), instead of a persisted lock that needs explicit operator action.
Tracking the 'peak' only since the EA was loaded or only while flat (71583, 8594, 11585), so a trailing drawdown reference depends on when the EA was started.
Rolling the day on the server calendar date only, with no configurable reset hour and no handling of a terminal that was off at rollover, so the day does not match the rule being mirrored.
Persistence keys that omit account login, server, magic or a tester prefix, so accounts, strategies or backtests overwrite each other's state.
Enforcing only in OnTick, so a quiet symbol or closed market delays the check; no timer or trade-event path.
Hard-coded constants and oversized defaults (balance floor of 1000 in 57272, 30% floating-loss default in 71645, 80% equity stop in 8594) instead of inputs sized from a risk policy.
Thresholds in account currency that do not scale with account size, lot size or volatility.
Using basket money targets, equity-ratio targets and basket loss cuts as the only exit for averaging baskets with no per-trade stop, which hides tail risk behind a smooth equity curve.
Treating daily profit targets and equity giveback trails as protection and optimising them, when they are fitted exit parameters.
Unthrottled logs, alerts and re-close loops that spam the journal or the trade server, and warnings without hysteresis that re-fire around the threshold.
Incrementing trade counters before the fill is confirmed, or not counting rejected setups, so quotas drift from reality.
Instant re-lock loop after a manual unlock because the trigger is not disarmed until the loss has receded.
Relying on a tick-emulated money stop or attaching stops late instead of guaranteeing a broker-side stop on every position, leaving the account unprotected when the terminal is offline.

features.name: Daily loss limit on equity (closed + floating) with configurable day boundary
features.rationale: The most common protection in the sample and the one that most directly bounds a bad day. It is a risk-budget rule, not a signal, so it adds little curve-fitting surface if the limit comes from risk policy or a prop rule rather than from optimisation. Must be equity-based: the balance-only versions (77167, 77220, 56126) ignore open losses. The intraday peak-drawdown variant (74840, 63193: lock when equity falls Y% from the day's equity peak) is a stricter optional mode that adds a parameter; keep it behind a flag. Depends on the history-rebuilt reference, the persisted lock and the latched flatten to be trustworthy.

features.name: Day reference rebuilt from deal history (deposit-aware, scoped)
features.rationale: Removes the single biggest weakness of the in-memory snapshot designs: a restart, recompile, VPS migration or a terminal that was off at rollover silently resets the daily baseline and hands the bot a fresh loss budget. Deriving the reference from the broker's own ledger is deterministic and works identically in the Strategy Tester, which keeps tests honest. No tunable parameters. Skipped checks should be surfaced in the status line; a conservative build can also hold new entries while history is unreadable.

features.name: Total drawdown limit: static floor or trailing equity high-water mark
features.rationale: This is the ruin stop: the point at which the strategy is assumed broken and a human must decide. Both prop-firm rule types (static and trailing) are covered by one enum. The peak must be persisted; several sources track it only since EA start (71583, 8594) or only while flat (11585), which makes the reference depend on when the EA was loaded. Auto-release when drawdown recovers to half the limit (71583) defeats the purpose and should not be copied. The limit is a policy number, not something to optimise.

features.name: Act-before-limit buffer on credit-free equity
features.rationale: A limit that fires exactly at the threshold is already breached by the time positions are closed. The buffer is a one-line change with no fitting value in a backtest (it only makes the guard more conservative). Subtracting credit prevents a broker bonus from masking real losses. Choosing the higher reference when in doubt errs on the safe side.

features.name: Crash-proof persisted lock state machine
features.rationale: Every account-level guard is worthless if a restart forgets that it fired; 'needs persistence' is the most repeated defect note in the raw ideas. Best practice across the high-quality sources: until-timestamp instead of a boolean (78702, 79035), level that only escalates (79430), tester keys isolated from live (79372), commit-marker writes (79017), unlock input that then refuses to start (78702), and re-arm hysteresis after a manual unlock so it does not instantly re-lock (73870). Implementation caveat: terminal global variables are dropped after about four weeks without access, so a permanent lock should be refreshed periodically or mirrored to a file. Never implement the halt by simulating keystrokes (14773).

features.name: Latched flatten with enforcement until flat
features.rationale: A one-shot close loop leaves positions open whenever a single request fails; the latch-until-flat pattern (22827) plus event-driven enforcement (79372, 73870, 79035) makes the halt real. Pending orders must be deleted too, otherwise they fill after the flatten. The lock must also gate the bot's own entry path, or it simply re-enters. Rate limiting and log throttling prevent a retry storm. In a single-strategy bot, enforcement should cover only its own magic; closing everything on the account is appropriate only for a deliberately account-wide guard.

features.name: Stop-loss watchdog for naked positions
features.rationale: Position sizing assumes the stop exists; a failed SL placement or modify silently converts a fixed-risk trade into unlimited risk. The best version (78343) escalates from re-attach to forced close, and 78982 adds a grace timer and alert. Restrict to own magic so manual trades and other EAs are not altered (8366 and 22001 touch everything). Auto-attaching a default TP is not part of protection and can be left out. No strategy parameters, so no fitting risk.

features.name: Early-warning alerts and visible block reasons
features.rationale: Does not change trading behaviour, so it cannot be curve-fitted, but it is what makes the bot auditable: every skipped entry and every halt has a stated cause that can be reconciled between tester and live (75652's short block code, 79035's trigger reason). Hysteresis and persistence stop alert spam around the threshold. Push/email channels can stay optional; the reason codes and throttled log are the v1 part.

features.name: Trade-frequency caps: daily/session quota, entry cooldown, one-setup-per-day key
features.rationale: Primarily a runaway guard: it bounds the damage of a logic bug or a whipsaw that keeps re-triggering entries, and it caps spread and commission bleed. Keep the cap a generous safety ceiling fixed in advance; once it is tuned on a backtest it becomes a fitted filter, hence the moderate overfitting score. The skip-marks-day key (78293) is a clean way to avoid retrying a setup that was rejected for stop width or lot size. All sources keep counters in memory; that must be fixed.

features.name: Consecutive-loss breaker and post-loss re-entry restraint
features.rationale: Sensible as a regime circuit breaker, but the daily loss limit already bounds the money at risk, and the streak length and cooldown window are easily fitted to past data. The size-escalation rule only matters if sizing can grow after losses; a bot with fixed-fractional sizing and no martingale gets it for free. Add later behind a flag, with the value chosen by policy rather than optimisation.

features.name: Exposure caps: positions, per-direction levels, single direction, entry spacing
features.rationale: Bounds worst-case simultaneous open risk regardless of what the signal logic does, and is the structural barrier against drifting into averaging. The sources that have it are mostly grids capping their own levels (79021); for a stop-based bot the useful form is a low total-position cap plus spacing so repeated signals do not stack at one price (17465). Fixed by policy; the spacing fraction is the only value that could be fitted.

features.name: Account precondition gates: live-arming guard, minimum capital, margin level
features.rationale: Three cheap gates with no fitting value. The arming guard (27428, originally licence code) keeps an untested build off a live account. The capital floor stops the bot when the account is too small for minimum lot size to respect the risk rule (57272 hard-codes it; make it an input). The margin-level gate (78982) prevents entries that would move the account toward broker stop-out. Each should emit a block reason.

features.name: Profit-target lock (challenge target / daily profit stop / equity ceiling)
features.rationale: Two different things share this mechanism. A permanent lock on reaching a prop-challenge target is legitimate and cannot be fitted: stopping once the objective is met removes pointless risk. A daily profit stop is not protection; it truncates the best days, and the threshold is a classic optimised parameter that flatters a backtest. Ship the challenge-target lock behind a flag; keep the daily variant disabled and out of any optimisation. The 're-arm from new balance' form (58462) is just a repeating basket take-profit.

features.name: Floating-loss circuit breaker (position and strategy scope, net of costs)
features.rationale: In the sources this is mostly the only loss control of grid and martingale baskets (11585, 12220, 72278, 71645 with a 30% default), which is the wrong use. As a last-resort layer behind hard per-trade stops it has some value: it catches a failed stop modification or correlated losses across symbols. It is largely redundant with the daily loss limit plus SL watchdog, and it only works while the terminal is running, so it must never replace broker-side stops. Express limits in % of equity, not account currency. In MQL5 take commission from the entry deals, since the position-level commission property is deprecated.

features.name: Basket money / equity-ratio take-profit close-all
features.rationale: Popular (11 EAs) but it is an exit strategy dressed as protection. It exists to harvest averaging baskets that have no per-trade stop, producing a smooth equity curve with an unbounded tail. Currency thresholds do not scale with lot size, account size or volatility, and the target is highly sensitive to optimisation. A stop-based bot should take profit per trade from its own exit logic; an account-level money target cuts across it and makes results hard to attribute. Only the net-of-swap-and-commission accounting is worth reusing.

features.name: Equity / basket profit giveback ratchet
features.rationale: An account-level trailing take-profit, not a survival mechanism. The arm threshold and giveback percent are fitted to the path of past equity curves and interact with the per-trade exits in ways that make a backtest look better without adding robustness. One of the three implementations is described as broken (12641) and none persist the peak. If profit protection is wanted, trail the stop of the individual position, where the logic is testable per trade.

features.name: Scheduled-event de-risking: Friday cutoff and pre-news flatten
features.rationale: The Friday entry cutoff is cheap, parameter-light and defensible; it could be enabled early. The pre-news flatten depends on an external event calendar and a breakeven band that is a fitted money parameter (58462 uses currency units), and the terminal's built-in economic calendar is not available in the Strategy Tester, so the behaviour cannot be honestly backtested without a separately maintained event file. Keep the news part out of v1 and never optimise the band.

features.name: Grid-basket rescue devices (indicator shock exit, order-count sync, late-stage profit lock)
features.rationale: All three come from the lowest-quality code in the sample (quality 1) and solve problems a stop-based bot does not have. The CCI threshold is an arbitrary fitted number that exits at the extreme of an impulse; the order-count trigger is a side-effect heuristic that breaks on any partial close; the late-stage lock is a patch on an exposure cap that should simply be lower. Adopting them imports the grid mindset and its hidden tail risk.

common_mistakes: Two-step entry (send naked, then attach SL/TP) without checking the modify result, without retries and without an emergency close, leaving positions unprotected (27964, 10925, 17373, 913, 17306).
Treating a broker-reported stops level or freeze level of 0 as 'no minimum distance'; ignoring the live spread and the freeze level entirely.

Applying a percentage safety multiplier to the stops level (x1.2, x1.5, x4) with no spread term, which stays 0 when the broker reports 0; or using tiny fixed fallbacks (5 or 10 points) that are below a normal gold spread.
Widening SL/TP to the broker minimum but not recomputing the lot size afterwards, so actual risk exceeds the intended risk (62732).
Applying the minimum-distance formula to absolute prices instead of distances (39402), or measuring stop distance from the wrong side of the quote (ask instead of bid for a long's SL/TP).
Normalising prices to _Digits only instead of SYMBOL_TRADE_TICK_SIZE, and comparing doubles for equality instead of using a half-tick tolerance.
Hard-coding the filling mode (FOK or IOC) and the order time type instead of deriving them from the symbol, so the EA never trades or cannot close on another broker.
Calling OrderCheck but sending the order anyway when it fails (49448), or not logging the check retcode and comment.
Applying margin/OrderCheck gates to closing or reducing orders, which can block an exit when margin is already short.
Retry loops with no attempt cap or no quote refresh (14833, 14869), and long Sleep calls inside the tick handler (up to 70 s in 11449) that freeze all other management.
Re-sending a failing entry on every tick of the entry window, or continuing to hammer the server after MARKET_CLOSED / TRADE_DISABLED with no backoff.
Trusting the boolean return of a trade call: clearing signal flags, counting a trade or counting an exit before the deal/position state was read back; ignoring partial fills.
Checking only PositionsTotal before entry, with no in-flight order guard, no timeout de-duplication and no restart-safe ownership scan, leading to duplicate positions.

Lot handling errors: rejecting instead of rounding to step (48251), silently clamping up to minimum lot when the risk-sized lot is smaller (62248), assuming two decimals of lot precision, and not announcing when traded size differs from requested size.

Using margin as the sizing basis (e.g. a fixed share of free margin) instead of only as a cap on a risk-sized lot; crude margin tests such as MODE_MARGINREQUIRED x lot against equity (14206) or a margin check that only runs on a tester dummy order (70900).

Hard-coded pip units and name-based metal detection, fixed pip thresholds (e.g. 2-pip trail step) and chart-symbol globals used while managing other symbols, all of which break across brokers, digits and price levels.

Per-tick trailing with no no-change check, no minimum improvement step, no freeze check and no throttle, producing modify spam and NO_CHANGES / TOO_MANY_REQUESTS errors; writing a freeze-level helper and never calling it (19963).

Hard-coded trading hours instead of the broker session table, no handling of sessions that wrap midnight, entries just before the daily break, and time exits scheduled at the close where they can be refused.
Acting on zero or stale quotes and on incomplete indicator buffers after reconnects or at session open.
Flatten routines that close positions before deleting pendings, iterate over a live list while closing, make a single pass with no leftover check, and never alert when they fail to get flat.

Pending orders with no server-side expiry and client-side-only OCO, buy stops not adjusted for spread, orders placed when price is already through the level, and no margin reserved for outstanding pendings.
Converting a rejected pending into a market order or auto-switching stop/limit type, which changes the strategy's semantics outside the backtest.
Relying on a static deviation value as slippage protection, with no pre-send price-drift check and no post-fill risk check.
Skipping trades silently: gates with no reason codes or logging, so differences between live and backtest behaviour cannot be diagnosed.
No measurement of realised stop slippage or real commission/swap, so backtest assumptions about gold and silver execution costs are never verified.
