features.name: Composite minimum stop-distance engine (stops level, freeze level, spread fallback, correct quote side)
features.rationale: The most common idea in the category (about 60 EAs) and here popularity matches merit: it removes invalid-stops rejections, which cluster exactly when spread widens. Keep k and the pad as fixed constants, never optimised. Two rules most sources miss: recompute lot size after any widening (62732 does not), and if the broker minimum would push the stop materially beyond the strategy stop, skip the trade instead of silently trading a different geometry. Percentage safety multipliers on a reported 0 (x1.2, x1.5, x4) remain 0, so the spread term is the real floor. Use a clamp helper for initial stops and a validate-only helper for trailing (19963).

features.name: Tick-size price rounding and instrument-scaled distance units
features.rationale: Cheap, deterministic, and it is what lets one code base run on XAUUSD and XAGUSD and across brokers with different digits. Percent-of-price or volatility-scaled inputs also reduce curve fitting because a parameter keeps its meaning across price regimes. The name-based metal pip table (11449) solves the same problem but is brittle against symbol suffixes and broker naming; derive everything from symbol properties instead.

features.name: Broker capability probe at init (filling mode, expiration type, account mode, input validation)
features.rationale: Hard-coded FOK/IOC is the single most frequent cause of an EA that simply never trades on a new broker. CTrade::SetTypeFillingBySymbol plus SetMarginMode covers the simple case; the bitmask plus execution-mode derivation (63916, 26324) is the more complete version. Failing fast at init with an explicit message is better than discovering a bad lot or filling mode at the first signal. No tunable parameters, so no fitting risk.

features.name: Pre-trade permission and broker-limit gate with distinct reason codes
features.rationale: Turns broker rejections into deliberate, explained skips, which is what makes live-versus-backtest differences diagnosable. The custom error enum from the cTrade pipelines (26451, 26418, 26315, 26324) is the valuable part: without reason codes a gate is just a silent filter. Keep it purely about permissions and limits; do not let strategy filters creep into it.

features.name: Volume normalisation and margin affordability check
features.rationale: Seen in about 54 EAs and genuinely necessary, but with a survival caveat: the lot must come from risk sizing and margin may only ever reduce it. If the risk-sized lot is below the minimum lot, skip the trade; falling back to minimum lot (62248) silently exceeds the risk budget. Fail closed when OrderCalcMargin itself fails (77180). Announcing the clamp with its size multiple (77060) keeps risk honest. The margin reserve is a fixed constant, not an optimisation input.

features.name: OrderCheck preflight inside the send path
features.rationale: A free server-rule simulation that catches margin, volume and stop errors before they reach the broker. Putting it in an overridden OrderSend (78968) guarantees no code path can bypass it, and the close/reduce exemption is essential: a preflight must never block an exit. It complements rather than replaces the stop-distance and session gates, since market-closed and frozen states only surface at send time.

features.name: Market-availability gate: broker session table, quote freshness, data readiness
features.rationale: Avoids acting on empty or stale quotes after reconnects and stops the EA from hammering a closed market. Reading the broker's own session table is more robust than hard-coded hours and handles DST and broker differences. Keep the pre-close cutoff a fixed constant (15 minutes in 77639), not an optimised input. The quote-age test must be neutral in the Strategy Tester, where ticks are synthetic, so it does not create a live/backtest difference.

features.name: Protected entry: stops anchored to the real fill, fail-safe close, slippage tolerance
features.rationale: The fail-safe close is what separates the good implementations (77639, 77691, 77167, 77220) from the many two-step entries that never check the modify (27964, 10925, 17373, 913). Prefer the atomic form where possible because the naked window is itself a risk; use two-step only as a fallback for brokers that reject stops on market execution. Pick one re-anchoring rule (SL at planned level with TP recomputed, or constant distance as in 71583) and use the same path in tester and live. A dynamic deviation equal to current spread (611) is a minor addition; the drift guard (14085) does the real work.

features.name: Safe modify/close wrapper: freeze-level guard, no-change skip, minimum step, throttle
features.rationale: Trailing and breakeven loops are the main source of request spam and TOO_MANY_REQUESTS/NO_CHANGES errors; this wrapper removes them without changing strategy logic. The freeze check must look at the existing level first (46309), since the server refuses modification of a frozen order regardless of the new value. Express the minimum step as a volatility fraction or tick multiple with a fixed value; do not optimise it. Emergency closes may bypass the throttle but not the freeze check.

features.name: Retcode-classified retry and backoff with attempt budgets
features.rationale: A table-driven policy replaces both failure modes seen in the sources: unbounded retry loops (14833, 14869) and every-tick resending of a failing entry (fixed in 77060 by stamping the attempt before sending). The asymmetry is deliberate: a missed entry costs nothing, an unexecuted exit can cost the account. Implement backoff with timestamps (retry_after per ticket, as in 79017 and 70900), not long Sleep calls inside the tick handler as in the MT4-era wrappers. Before any entry retry, re-run the spread and drift checks.

features.name: Read-back confirmation of fills, modifies and closes
features.rationale: The EA's internal state (position count, daily trade counter, risk used) is only as honest as its confirmation step. 78343's read-back for SL and close is the cleanest version; 12220's deal-count polling solves the same problem with Sleep and should be replaced by OnTradeTransaction or next-tick re-checks. Risk accounting must use the filled volume, not the requested one.

features.name: Duplicate-entry prevention and restart-safe ownership
features.rationale: Double entries are a classic silent risk multiplier and come from three distinct causes that each need their own guard: async fill latency (in-flight check, 26418/26315), timeouts followed by blind retry (9086), and restarts that lose in-memory state (78715). Keep cooldowns short and execution-only so they do not become an untested strategy filter. The MT4 GlobalVariable trade-context mutex (7876) is not needed in MT5; a shared lock is only relevant if several EAs draw on one risk budget.

features.name: Emergency flatten routine (snapshot, pendings first, retry until flat)
features.rationale: A daily-loss or kill-switch rule is only real if the flatten path is robust; the two quality-5 guards (78702, 79035) show the needed pieces: stable ticket snapshot, pendings before positions, persistence while halted, rate limiting and an alert when it cannot finish. Closing by position ticket (62811) is hedging-safe. No tunable strategy parameters.

features.name: Pending-order lifecycle hygiene (side validity, spread-adjusted trigger, expiry, OCO)
features.rationale: Not needed if v1 enters at market on closed bars, but mandatory the moment any pending order is used: an orphaned straddle leg or a stale stop order is a real account risk. Server-side expiry (13509) protects when the terminal is offline, whereas OCO cancellation is client-side and can fail in exactly that case. Counting margin of existing pendings (17465) prevents a fill that the account cannot support. Stale-pending requoting within one tick (13233) is an HFT exchange technique and should not be carried over.

features.name: Execution-cost telemetry: stop slippage, fill slippage, real commission and swap
features.rationale: Low count but high value for the stated goal of honest testability: it is the only mechanism in the category that measures how far live execution departs from the backtest. It is passive, has no parameters and cannot be curve-fitted. Reading costs from deals (74840) is preferable to inferring commission from one past trade (11449), which is fragile.

features.name: Virtual (hidden) SL/TP enforced by the EA instead of the server
features.rationale: As the stop mechanism it hides risk: there is no protection when the terminal, VPS or connection is down or the EA is throttled, and the tester closes virtual stops at the trigger tick with no latency, making the backtest more optimistic than live. It also contradicts the 'no position without a confirmed server-side stop' invariant. Single source of modest quality. If a virtual exit is ever added, risk must be sized on the server-side stop distance.

features.name: Pending-to-market fallback and automatic order-type switching
features.rationale: It silently changes what the strategy is: a breakout stop becomes a late chase at market with a worse entry and smaller R, and a stop that turns into a limit inverts the trade logic from momentum to fade. Live behaviour then diverges from what was tested, and the divergence appears only in fast markets. Auto type selection is reasonable for a manual panel where a human chose the price, not for an automated entry.

features.name: Close-by netting and double-lot reversal (OrderCloseBy)
features.rationale: It presupposes holding opposite positions at once, which a survival-first single-direction bot should never do, and the double-lot reversal briefly overshoots exposure and margin; if the second step fails the account is left with an unintended position. The benefit is one spread, the cost is account-mode dependence and an extra failure path. Both sources are MT4-era and low quality. A plain close followed by a normally gated new entry is safer and testable.

common_mistakes: Thresholds in fixed points or pips (max spread, range width, band width, previous-day range, one-bar move). They do not transfer between gold and silver, between 2- and 3-digit quotes, or across years in which gold's price level changed several-fold; use fractions of ATR or of the trade's own stop distance.
Session hours hard-coded in raw server time with no DST handling, so 'London open' or 'New York open' is an hour off for part of every year and differs between brokers.

Deriving the server offset from TimeTradeServer()-TimeGMT() or building windows on TimeGMT. This works live but in the Strategy Tester TimeGMT equals server time, so the backtest runs different hours from live.

Relying on the MT5 calendar for a news filter without a tester source. Calendar functions are unavailable in the Strategy Tester, so the filter is silently inactive in every backtest and the tested bot is not the traded bot.

Detecting news currencies by slicing the symbol name into 3-letter halves or by substring match. This fails on GOLD, suffixed symbols and XAU/XAG (which have no events); metals need an explicit map to USD.
Fetching third-party calendar pages with WebRequest inside the trading EA: trading blocks on the network, the feed's time zone is easy to misread, and the result cannot be backtested.
Reading SYMBOL_SPREAD / MODE_SPREAD or a single tick sample instead of measuring Ask-Bid at the moment of order placement, and ignoring commission in the cost check.
Applying spread or session gates to exits and protective logic, or pairing a spread-gated soft exit with no server-side stop. Filters should block new risk, never the ability to get out.

Time-window code that breaks when start > end (midnight wrap), has hour-only resolution, or leaves equal start/end undefined; hard-coding 'hour 0' as rollover or a Friday hour regardless of the broker's clock.

One-trade-per-day and per-window latches kept only in memory and reset at server hour 0. A restart re-arms them and the bot repeats the trade; state must be persisted and rebuilt from positions and deal history.

Stacking many thresholded regime filters (ATR floors and ceilings, band width, ADX, volume ratios, distance bands, day-of-week skips) without a no-filter control. Each adds parameters, shrinks the sample and makes the backtest a fit.

Using volatility or news filters to make grid, martingale or recovery sizing look safe (several source EAs gate grid adds this way). A filter reduces how often the tail is hit; it does not remove the tail.

Tick-based detectors (tick velocity, tick speed, N-tick spread averages) and tick-volume filters treated as if they were portable. They depend on the broker's feed and the tester's tick model, and tick volume on OTC metals is not real volume.
Silent vetoes: skipped trades are not logged with a reason, so live and backtest results cannot be reconciled and nobody knows which filter is doing the work.
Evaluating filters on the forming bar or on indicators that repaint, and creating indicator handles repeatedly instead of once in OnInit with closed-bar reads.
Flatten logic that fires on every tick while a condition holds, or that closes positions inside the rollover or pre-news spread spike, instead of once per event and ahead of the widening.
Day-based filters computed on D1 bars that include Sunday stub bars or an inconsistent day boundary, which corrupts ATR, NR4/NR7 and previous-day range tests.
Querying the calendar only for 'today', which misses events shortly after server midnight, or refreshing it either every tick (slow) or once a day (stale, misses revised times).
Trading the news with stop-order straddles and trusting the backtest, which does not model release-time spread widening and slippage.
Testing spread-sensitive rules on generated ticks or a fixed tester spread; spread gates and cost ratios are only meaningful on real-tick data.

features.name: News blackout from the native MT5 economic calendar
features.rationale: Scheduled USD releases are the most predictable source of spread blow-outs and stop slippage on metals, and the native calendar needs no WebRequest or DLL. The best examples (75652, 76605) cache the result and never block position management. Keep the windows fixed a priori (e.g. 30 min before / 30 min after for high impact) and do not optimise them. Flatten-before-news stays behind a flag because closing into a widening spread has its own cost. This is only honest if paired with the tester-compatible source in the next feature.

features.name: Tester-compatible news source: calendar CSV replay and date blacklist
features.rationale: Without this the live bot runs a news filter that the backtest never exercised, so the tested system and the traded system differ. 76605 shows the CSV fallback with a GMT-to-server offset; 64444 shows the trivial date blacklist; 68215/58462/16308 show the cache-to-file pattern (their WebRequest scraping itself is unnecessary on MT5 and should not be in the trading EA). The minimum acceptable v1 is the explicit 'news filter inactive in this run' log line plus a blacklist of release dates.

features.name: News straddle / event breakout trading (OCO stops around releases)
features.rationale: A backtest of a straddle around a release is not trustworthy: the tester does not reproduce the spread widening, stop-order slippage and partial liquidity of the release second, so the result measures the tester's fill model rather than an edge. It also adds a second strategy with its own risk budget to a bot whose first goal is survival. Seen only in quality 2-3 EAs. The news calendar should be used to stand aside, not to trade.

features.name: Cost-relative spread gate with hard cap, entry-only
features.rationale: The most consistently good idea in the category and present in the highest-quality EAs (77691, 78259, 77639, 78778). Expressing cost as a fraction of the trade's own risk unit is scale-free, tightens automatically when the stop is small, and needs no per-symbol tuning, unlike the fixed point caps of older EAs. One parameter, chosen a priori. It must never block protective exits, and every veto must be logged.

features.name: Empirical execution-cost baseline (spread and slippage recorder) and adaptive cap
features.rationale: As a measurement tool it is low-risk and valuable: it replaces guessed thresholds with broker-specific data (79460 is quality 5). As a live adaptive gate it adds state, depends on tick feed, and can normalise bad conditions (k x 'normal rollover spread' accepts a spread that should be refused). So: run the recorder alongside v1, keep the gate thresholds fixed, and put any adaptive cap or slippage-based pause behind a flag later. Session-scaled caps (69651) add tunable multipliers for little gain.

features.name: Tradability gate: broker session table, pre-close margin, rollover blackout, stale-quote check
features.rationale: Pure hygiene with no fitted parameters: it removes 'market closed' rejections, orders sent into the daily break, and decisions taken on a frozen price. Reading the broker's own table (77691, 78891, 61921, 17465) is more robust than hard-coded hours such as 'skip server hour 0' (69651), which is wrong on any broker with a different offset. The stale-quote test (79460, 15708) is one comparison per tick.

features.name: Entry time window with midnight wrap (minute resolution, per weekday)
features.rationale: The most common filter in the set and trivial to get right, but most implementations are hour-only, server-time-only, or mishandle start > end. It belongs in v1 as plain plumbing. The risk is not the code but the use: optimising start/end hours is a classic curve fit, so windows should come from market structure (London, New York) and be fed by the DST-aware engine. Per-weekday strings are flexible but multiply the parameters; keep them fixed.

features.name: DST-aware session anchoring and rule-based server offset
features.rationale: Required for honest testing of any session-based logic: without it a 'London open' rule is an hour off for part of every year, and backtest and live disagree. The quality 4-5 examples (78259, 17465, 68082) compute DST by rule; the auto-detect and TimeGMT approaches (79460, 77180, 76605) are fine live but collapse in the tester, where TimeGMT equals server time. 78702 shows the same offset logic reused for a configurable day boundary with self-tests, which is the right standard.

features.name: Scheduled flatten and week-edge guards (Friday cutoff, weekly-open wait, daily flat time)
features.rationale: A stop-loss does not protect across a gap, so not opening fresh risk into the weekend and not trading the first minutes of the weekly open are cheap survival rules with no fitted edge. The daily flat time depends on strategy style (intraday yes, H4 swing no), so it is an input, but the scheduler must exist and be exactly-once (78968) rather than 'if hour > 18 close' on every tick (8595). Monday-skip toggles (7612, 18704) are day-of-week fitting and should not be optimised.

features.name: Setup-geometry sanity band normalised by ATR
features.rationale: This is a validity check on the trade rather than a predictive filter: a stop inside the noise or a range several times normal makes the risk unit meaningless and distorts position sizing. The good examples (75586, 77639, 77094, 78293) all normalise by ATR; the older ones (18704, 21452) use fixed points and are not portable. Keep the band wide and fixed. A plain ATR is enough for v1; blended ADR (24786) or MA-smoothed ATR (11739) are refinements, and the range-derived step with clamps (11585, 12872) came from grid spacing and is not adopted for that purpose.

features.name: Closed-bar volatility shock pause (ATR ratio / bar range versus ATR)
features.rationale: The calendar only covers scheduled events; this is the one shock guard that also catches unscheduled moves and behaves identically in backtest and live. Use it as a circuit breaker with one conservative ceiling fixed a priori, kept out of the optimiser and compared against a no-filter run. Caveats: for breakout entries expansion is the signal, so apply only an extreme ceiling there; the floor, volume ratios and session-specific multipliers (69651), the +/-61.8% blended band (17465) and the indicator-based volatmeter (9499) add parameters and should stay off in v1. In 62684 it gated grid adds, which does not make a grid safe.

features.name: Tick-velocity fast-market detector with cooldown
features.rationale: Reacts faster than any closed-bar filter, but its behaviour depends on the broker's tick feed and on the tester's tick model, so it is not reproducible without real-tick data and is easy to tune to one feed. Its best-known example (76605) is a recovery EA where it also widens grid spacing, i.e. it was compensating for risky money management. If used, start in log-only mode and compare flags against the closed-bar shock pause before letting it gate trades.

features.name: Compression/expansion day filters (NR4/NR7, yesterday range versus ADR, Bollinger width)
features.rationale: A legitimate, published idea, and 78259 (quality 5) implements it properly with a control group. But it is a predictive regime filter with many variants and thresholds, it cuts the trade count sharply, and choosing the variant after seeing results is curve fitting. Add it only after the unfiltered v1 is characterised, one variant at a time. The Bollinger-width versions (11472, 25848, 16350) use fixed point widths and are redundant with an ATR-relative measure; the fixed 150-point previous-day kill (8417) is unusable as written.

features.name: Higher-timeframe trend/regime agreement gate
features.rationale: Direction bias is part of the strategy definition, not of the protective filter layer, and each variant (EMA stack, ADX/DI, SuperTrend, Alligator, DEMA slope) brings periods and thresholds to tune. If the entry logic needs a bias, pick the simplest one a priori and keep the 'none' mode for comparison. The four-state ADX switch that routes between trend and mean-reversion strategies (9499) doubles the system to be validated and is not for v1. 74894 applied the gate only to add-on entries; it should cover all entries or none.

features.name: Over-extension filter (distance from baseline in ATR)
features.rationale: A reasonable entry-quality rule that also keeps the stop distance sane, but it is one more threshold and it removes exactly the strongest momentum trades, so its net effect is strategy-specific and must be shown against a control. 74840 uses a raw distance in points and adds a slope requirement; 71645 bundles it with ATR-expansion, price-velocity and tick-volume scores, which is a stack of fitted thresholds. Only the single ATR-distance form (28117) is worth carrying.

features.name: Attempt limiter: one attempt per day/window plus entry cooldown, persisted
features.rationale: Caps how much damage a bad day or a signal loop can do and makes trade counts predictable, with no fitted edge. Almost every example keeps the latch in memory (214, 68125, 18704), so a restart or VPS reboot re-arms it and the bot trades the same setup twice; persistence and reconstruction from trade history are the actual feature. Cooldowns should be in seconds or bars of a named timeframe, not PeriodSeconds of whatever chart the EA sits on (22705).

features.name: Gate pipeline with reason codes, veto logging and per-filter switches
features.rationale: This is what makes the other filters honestly testable. Logged vetoes (77060) let live and backtest be reconciled trade by trade; a visible block reason (72527, 78778, 11449) explains why the bot is idle; a FILTER_NONE control (78259) shows whether a filter adds anything or just removes trades. Without it, filters accumulate silently and nobody can tell which one produced the equity curve.

features.name: Self-calibrating and pseudo-statistical filters
features.rationale: Each looks rigorous but rests on too little data or on re-fitting inside the bot. A direction switch based on which side recently simulated better (19392) is performance chasing with hidden parameters and cannot be validated out of sample because it keeps changing. Twenty returns give a drift estimate that is mostly noise (73622). A POC from close counts without real volume (62713) is not a volume profile; its own reader noted it would need real volume to mean anything. All come from quality 2-3 EAs and all add opaque state that makes test results hard to interpret.

common_mistakes: Keeping trade state only in memory (static/global variables): a restart re-enters on the same bar or session, re-fires a partial-TP level, or orphans open positions.
Consuming the new-bar latch before indicator data and quotes are validated, so the bar's signal is silently skipped on a cold start or failed CopyBuffer.
The opposite error: rewinding the bar stamp on any OrderSend/OrderModify failure, which retries every tick with no attempt cap and no error classification and re-runs steps that already succeeded.

Sending a new order before the previous one is confirmed (treating the OrderSend return as proof a position exists), giving duplicate entries on asynchronous fills; or using a waiting flag with no timeout, which can block the bot forever.
Reading a deal inside OnTradeTransaction before it and its order are selectable in history, and relying on events alone with no polling reconciliation or startup resync.
Scanning by symbol only, or by comment or 'has an SL', and so managing manual trades or another EA's trades; counting open positions but forgetting pending orders when enforcing one-trade-at-a-time.
Auto-deriving the magic number from symbol characters or timeframe: collisions between symbols, and orphaned positions when the chart timeframe changes.

Capturing the day-start baseline while disconnected (zero balance, unset server time) or taking the current balance as baseline on a mid-day restart, which silently resets the daily loss limit; counting deposits/withdrawals as trading P/L.

Writing GlobalVariables without GlobalVariablesFlush (lost on a crash), never deleting per-ticket keys, sharing keys between tester and live, and saving state before the account is ready so good state is overwritten with garbage.
Using a GlobalVariable or a fixed seconds cooldown as the only duplicate-entry guard; it is lost on VPS migration and a 15-second cooldown confirms nothing.
Recomputing partial-close percentages from the already reduced volume after a restart, and restoring 'initial risk' from the current SL after it has been trailed or moved to breakeven.
One-shot close-all that is not retried: a partial failure leaves a half-flattened book, and entry logic keeps running while the flatten is incomplete.
Flattening positions in OnDeinit on chart, timeframe or parameter change instead of persisting state and resuming.
Trading on unvalidated indicator values (zero ATR, EMPTY_VALUE, too few bars, unsynchronised higher timeframe), which turns risk-based sizing into absurd lots.
No input validation and no hard risk ceiling: the optimiser explores nonsensical combinations and an operator typo becomes oversized risk.

Running all guards only in OnTick, so loss limits, timeouts and stop repair freeze when the chart symbol is quiet or the market is in its break; or the reverse, putting trading decisions on the timer so results depend on timer granularity.
Re-sending SL/TP modifies every tick with exact double comparison, or retrying a rejected breakeven indefinitely, producing 'no changes' errors and request storms.
Using new-bar detection on the chart timeframe when the signal timeframe is different.
Using loss detection or streak state to escalate lot size (martingale) rather than to cool down or reduce risk.
Level-triggered alerts on every tick instead of edge-triggered alerts with recovery messages, so real failures drown in spam; no signal when the bot itself stops.
External news data fetched per tick or per restart with no cache, WebRequest whitelist errors not distinguished from transport errors, and stale data not visible - the filter silently stops working.
Checking trade permissions only in OnInit and never again, and allowing a second instance on the same symbol and magic with no instance lock.

features.name: Ownership by symbol + magic + position identifier
features.rationale: Without strict ownership every other safeguard (recovery, flatten, stop repair) can act on trades it does not own. Cheap, deterministic and identical in tester and live. Keep the magic an explicit input: magics hashed from the symbol name (62248) can collide, and ones that encode the timeframe (7876) orphan positions when the chart timeframe changes. Comment matching (16136) is unreliable. Symbol-only tracking breaks on hedging accounts.

features.name: Stateless restart recovery from broker state
features.rationale: Most robust form of restart safety: no file or variable can go stale, it survives VPS migration, and the same code path runs in the tester and live, so it is honestly testable. Two limits to respect: history must be synced before it is trusted (see startup preflight), and some state is not derivable - 77639 restores initial risk from the current SL, which is wrong once the stop has been moved; that part needs the durable store.

features.name: Persisted once-per-signal entry lock (GlobalVariable)
features.rationale: Seen in 7 EAs and cheap, but it duplicates what deal history states authoritatively. GlobalVariables are terminal-local (lost on VPS migration or reinstall), are purged after about four weeks without access and can be deleted by hand. Worth having as a write-ahead marker for the short window before history is synced and to block same-bar re-entry after a stop-out; not a v1 requirement if the history-derived guard exists.

features.name: Minimal durable store for non-derivable state
features.rationale: Without it a restart re-fires a partial-TP level, recomputes percentages from the reduced volume, loses the R basis for management, or forgets that a flatten was in progress. Keep the surface minimal so there is little to corrupt, and save nothing before the account is ready. 13942 flattens on chart/parameter change; persist instead. Tester keys must be isolated so backtests do not read live state.

features.name: Transaction-confirmed order state machine (in-flight guard + deferred deal queue)
features.rationale: Directly prevents duplicate entries on asynchronous fills, the most common live-only bug in these EAs. Events are a hint, not the source of truth: they are missed while disconnected, and a waiting flag without a timeout can block the bot indefinitely (63916 bounds the wait at 3x1000 ms, 79437 falls back after 10 s). 79437's deferred queue fixes the race where the deal is not yet selectable. Always pair with a startup resync (48222 lacks it).

features.name: Closed-bar gate that re-arms on data failure
features.rationale: Closed-bar evaluation removes intra-bar look-ahead and repainting, so 'open prices' or 1-minute-OHLC tests match live behaviour - the basis of honest testing. Committing the latch only after valid data avoids the silent 'signal skipped on cold start' bug that 14 EAs work around. The re-arm must cover data and permission failures only, not order failures (see bounded delivery).

features.name: Decide once, deliver with a bounded retry window and failure circuit breaker
features.rationale: 78343 is the best version. The naive form in six sources (10281, 8595, 8499, 11102, 17137 rewind the bar stamp on any OrderSend/OrderModify failure; 1397 commits only on success) retries every tick with no cap and no error classification and re-runs steps that already succeeded - popular but harmful: request floods on permanent errors and late fills from a stale signal. 78715's mark-before-act is the safe at-most-once extreme. Bounded delivery plus the in-flight guard gives retries without duplicates.

features.name: Market/indicator data sanity and history-readiness guards
features.rationale: Garbage indicator values on a cold start or after a history gap are a direct path to absurd lot sizes or false signals. The bounds are sanity limits, not tuning knobs: keep them wide, fixed and out of the optimiser. Every failure must be logged so a 'no trades' backtest can be explained rather than hidden.

features.name: Input validation and fail-fast init with a hard risk cap
features.rationale: Costs almost nothing and prevents the two worst operator errors: oversized risk and inverted or overlapping session settings. Ending invalid passes early also keeps the optimiser from wasting passes on, and occasionally 'finding', nonsensical combinations. Per-side open/close enable switches (15228) belong here as plain inputs and give an exit-only mode for winding the bot down.

features.name: Startup preflight: connection, permissions and account identity
features.rationale: State loaded or a baseline captured while disconnected is silently wrong and then persisted - 78680 and 73870 exist to stop exactly that. Checking permissions only in OnInit (12641, 14773) is not enough: AutoTrading can be switched off later, so gate each send and alert once. An account switch on the same terminal must not inherit the previous account's day lock or ticket state.

features.name: Single-instance lock with heartbeat
features.rationale: Protects against the operator error of attaching the bot twice to the same symbol and magic, which can double entries in the same tick before either instance sees the other's position. Only 2 EAs (both good quality) and it adds its own failure mode (stale lock, clock source), so keep it behind a flag; ownership filtering plus the in-flight guard already limit the damage. Not meaningful in the tester.

features.name: Trading-day rollover: baseline rebuild and daily state reset
features.rationale: A daily loss limit is only as good as its baseline: using the current balance at a mid-day restart silently resets the limit after losses (the survival failure 78680 and 79035 fix). The estimate from history must be flagged because floating P/L at day start cannot be fully reconstructed. The phase machine with 'orders placed once' keeps a session strategy from re-arming. 64444's refresh-after-N-bars adds a tunable parameter; prefer a fixed expiry tied to the session.

features.name: Idempotent SL/TP reconciliation and missing-stop repair
features.rationale: A position without a stop is unbounded risk; a convergence loop (desired vs actual) repairs it after restarts, failed first modifies and stop-less opens without having to track what failed. The tolerance compare (12220) avoids 'no changes' rejections and per-tick modify spam; 77639's attempt-once rule for breakeven avoids retry storms. Deterministic and identical in the tester.

features.name: Latched flatten: close-all retried until flat
features.rationale: Close-all loops partially fail in practice (requote, busy, market closed). Without a latch the trigger condition can disappear after the first partial close (profit falls back below target, equity recovers) and the rest is left open - a hidden-risk state. Three EAs use the same simple latch. Persist it so a restart continues flattening, and delete pendings so they cannot fill mid-flatten.

features.name: Timer plus tick processing with throttle
features.rationale: Guards that live only in OnTick stop when the chart symbol is quiet; a 1-second timer costs nothing. The discipline is to keep decisions off the timer: 244 runs all logic from the timer with a price-change gate, which makes results depend on timer granularity and tick modelling. Throttling (18709) reduces modify and request spam.

features.name: Edge-triggered health monitoring, heartbeat and self-audit
features.rationale: Does not change trading decisions, so it can follow v1, but the edge-triggered pattern is the right way to log state changes from day one (alert once, report recovery). The self-audit checks are independent verification that the dedup and ownership logic actually worked. Push notifications cannot be validated in the tester; test them on demo.

features.name: External data (news calendar) fetch robustness
features.rationale: Only needed if a news filter is added. The honest-testing problem is the main reason to defer it: WebRequest and the built-in calendar do not work in the Strategy Tester, so the filter's effect cannot be verified by backtest unless historical events are replayed from a file. If added, failures must be loud. The raw idea is MQL4 (error 4060); in MQL5 a non-whitelisted URL returns error 4014.

features.name: Fragile state carriers and hidden persisted settings/learned state
features.rationale: Each of these looked convenient in its source EA and each hides risk. Comment tags (71583, 16136) and SL-presence (51095) misidentify what the bot owns; chart objects (12598) disappear with a template change; balance snapshots (7891) confuse deposits, swaps and other EAs' trades with the bot's own result and were used for lot escalation. Persisted settings (75690, 19752) and learned tables (1108) make live behaviour irreproducible from the inputs and let tester pre-training leak into live.

common_mistakes: Judging a trade from DEAL_PROFIT or a balance change alone, leaving out entry-deal commission, swap and partial closes, or treating a vanished ticket as proof of the outcome instead of rebuilding the position from its deals.
Measuring R against the trailed or final stop instead of the initial stop, which makes every breakeven-managed trade look risk-free.
Reporting results only in points or account money across years in which the gold price and lot sizes changed several-fold, instead of R or basis points.
Showing win rate without the breakeven win rate implied by the stop/target geometry and costs, so a near target passes for an edge.

Optimistic bar-replay assumptions: counting the target first when one bar contains both stop and target, ignoring costs or modelling them by shifting the entry, and trusting M1 bar spread that understates real reopen spread by roughly 3x.

Measuring execution quality only around the EA's own OrderSend call (GetTickCount, price sent versus price filled), which misses stop-loss and take-profit exits where slippage is worst, and logging slippage without a sign convention.
Sending push, email or web requests from OnTick or OnTradeTransaction, blocking the trade path and hitting notification rate limits during bursts.

Log spam from a condition that blocks trading on every tick, or the opposite fix of printing only every Nth message, which drops events arbitrarily; also decision logs that can be switched off entirely.
CSV logs that rewrite or duplicate the header on restart, are not flushed per row, cannot be read while open, or write duplicate rows after a restart; one file shared by several symbols or instances.

Silently replacing invalid inputs with defaults, or handling impossible parameter combinations by returning from OnTick so zero-trade passes stay in the optimiser results instead of rejecting them in OnInit.
Hard-coding the symbol name or pip value, so a broker suffix or a different contract/tick specification for gold or silver breaks sizing without any error.
Optimising on raw profit or an ad-hoc scalar (win/loss counts, streak penalties, return rescaled to a target drawdown) with no minimum trade count.
Treating an in-run in-sample/out-of-sample split as a true holdout even though the optimiser selects on the out-of-sample score too.
Deriving hour, weekday or session filters from bucket tables of the same backtest, often with a handful of trades per bucket, and mixing broker server time with UTC when tagging sessions.
Reading an independent-resample Monte Carlo drawdown as a worst case, and using backtest-derived Kelly fraction or similar statistics to set position size.
Folding independent risk limits into one weighted score so a breached limit is diluted by the others, then using the score to scale lots.
Splitting the strategy into sub-models and optimising them stage by stage on the same history, hiding the real number of fitted parameters.
Never comparing the strategy with a random-entry baseline using the same exits, so exit geometry and market drift are credited to the signal.
Not logging the inputs of the lot calculation or comparing planned risk with realised loss, so sizing errors and gap losses are only discovered from the equity curve.

Leaving restart and persistence behaviour untested because the Strategy Tester cannot exercise it, and letting tester-only code branches change trading behaviour rather than only UI, sleeps and notifications.
Storing per-trade diagnostics in the order comment, which brokers truncate or overwrite.
Drawing panels, objects and Comment output during optimisation, slowing every pass for no benefit.

features.name: Position-level trade journal rebuilt from deals (net of all costs)
features.rationale: Every other statistic depends on a correct per-position net result. Entry-deal commission and swap are the costs most often dropped, which flatters win rate and expectancy. Running the identical journal in the tester and live is what makes backtest-versus-live reconciliation possible. The weaker variants (77094, 77220) only notice a vanished ticket and keep a running win rate; the 79024 deal-loop version is the one to copy.

features.name: R-multiple against the initial stop, plus MFE/MAE per trade
features.rationale: R against the original stop is the only unit that stays comparable across lot sizes, volatility regimes and price levels, and it exposes whether trailing or breakeven logic actually adds anything. MFE/MAE shows whether stops are too tight or targets unreachable. The risk is tuning SL/TP to the excursion distribution of the same sample, so treat it as a diagnostic and confirm any change on unseen data.

features.name: Session, weekday, hour and exit-reason tags with bucket tables
features.rationale: Tagging is cheap and makes results explainable: where the losses come from, how many exits were stop-outs, whether one session carries the whole result. The danger is the next step: building hour or weekday filters out of the same backtest table is plain data mining. Keep the tags in v1, but only accept a session filter that has a structural reason and survives out of sample. In the tester TimeGMT equals simulated server time, so the UTC offset must be an explicit input.

features.name: Execution-cost telemetry: signed slippage, fill latency and spread
features.rationale: Most of the gap between a backtest and a live account is execution cost, and it cannot be assumed, only measured. These numbers are what justify the spread, slippage and delay settings used in the tester. Nothing here can be curve-fitted. The MQL4-style variants (GetTickCount around OrderSend, slippage against the price the EA sent) miss stop exits, which is where slippage is worst. In v1 only record; do not let the bot adapt its behaviour to these numbers yet.

features.name: Decision journal with reason codes and a single order-send choke point
features.rationale: This is what makes the bot honestly testable: a backtest and a live run can be compared decision by decision, and a missing trade always has a stated cause. A single send wrapper is also the natural place for pre-trade validation and retcode handling. Count skips per reason at deinit so a filter that silently blocks most signals is visible. Do not carry telemetry in the order comment (15708): brokers truncate or overwrite it.

features.name: Risk audit: sizing line, planned-versus-realised loss, never-widen-stop check
features.rationale: Sizing errors are the most common way an EA destroys an account, and they are invisible unless every input to the lot calculation is printed. The realised/planned ratio turns gap and slippage risk into a measured number instead of an assumption. The stop-widening scan is a cheap invariant: a survival-first bot must never loosen a stop, and this proves it on every test run.

features.name: Logging plumbing: levels, change-based throttling, durable append-only CSV
features.rationale: The journals above are only useful if they are readable and survive restarts, crashes and a spreadsheet holding the file open. Change-based suppression keeps a condition that blocks trading tick after tick from flooding the log while losing no information. Avoid the 56773 variant that prints only every 500th message in the tester: it drops events arbitrarily and makes tester logs differ from live logs. Name files by symbol and magic so instances never share a file.

features.name: Tester and optimiser hygiene: strict input validation, no UI in tester
features.rationale: Silent defaulting means the test ran with parameters other than the ones shown, which is dishonest by construction. Rejecting nonsense combinations in OnInit is cleaner than returning early from OnTick (31582), which leaves zero-trade passes in the result table. Skipping UI only affects speed. The one rule to hold: tester-specific branches may skip drawing, sleeping and notifications, never anything that changes orders.

features.name: OnTester criterion with hard gates and early/late consistency
features.rationale: Left alone, the optimiser ranks by balance, which is the strongest invitation to curve fitting. Minimum-trade and no-losing-segment gates remove lucky low-sample passes; the sign-preserving form keeps losing passes ranked below zero. The limit must be stated plainly: the optimiser still selects on the late segment, so it is a consistency filter, not a holdout. Keep a separate untouched forward period and demo run. Source 63193 is low-quality code; take the idea, not the implementation, and set the trade-count gate well above its 20.

features.name: Cost-aware expectancy checks: breakeven win rate and pessimistic bar resolution
features.rationale: Showing the required win rate next to the achieved one is trivial to compute and immediately exposes setups whose high win rate comes only from a near target. The stop-first rule and charging costs on both sides are the conservative assumptions any internal simulation must use. What should stay out of v1 is the source EA's use of the replay to rank parameter combinations on the live chart: that is a hidden self-optimiser. Keep the report and the assumptions, not the live combo selection.

features.name: Random-entry benchmark mode (null hypothesis)
features.rationale: It answers the question a backtest alone cannot: how much of the result comes from the signal and how much from exit geometry, risk engine and market drift. It costs one input and a few lines, and it cannot be over-fitted because it has nothing to tune. A single random run proves nothing either way, so compare against a spread of seeds. The live-account guard is mandatory.

features.name: Built-in self-tests: known-answer checks and state round trip
features.rationale: MQL5 has no test framework, so the practical route is to keep risk and state logic in pure functions and ship the tests inside the EA. This catches regressions in exactly the code that protects the account (sizing, daily-loss state, restart recovery) before any market data is involved. It appears only in the highest-quality sources (78748, 79035, 79460), which is a signal in itself.

features.name: Timer-driven, rate-limited notifications and heartbeat
features.rationale: Useful for supervision but not part of survival logic, and it adds external dependencies (push limits, WebRequest allow-list, third-party endpoints). If added, the 78748 design is the only safe one: network calls block, so they must never sit in a trade path, and push limits make unbatched alerts fail exactly during bursts. Keep it one-way telemetry; a remote command channel is a different and riskier feature. DLL-based transports (1246) should not be used.

features.name: Trade-list robustness analytics: bootstrap Monte Carlo, distribution metrics, per-pass frames
features.rationale: It replaces the single backtest drawdown with a distribution, which is more honest, and frames let you inspect the whole population of passes instead of the top row. But resampling trades independently destroys loss clustering, so the drawdown and ruin figures are optimistic and must be read as a lower bound. The Kelly fraction from a backtest must never feed position sizing. It can all be done offline from the core CSV journal, so it does not need to be in v1.

features.name: Demo acceptance harness: restart-survival test and demo-only build
features.rationale: Restart behaviour cannot be exercised in the Strategy Tester, and state loss or duplicate orders after a terminal restart are real account risks, so this is the right test before going live. It is heavy to build and maintain, though, and the in-tester state round trip covers most of the persistence logic for v1. The DEMO_ONLY wrapper is nearly free and worth adopting early, since it avoids forking the source for test builds.

features.name: Count-based or drawdown-rescaled fitness formulas
features.rationale: Counting wins and losses ignores their size, so the formula rewards many small wins and hides the rare large loss; penalising streak length pushes the optimiser toward the same high-win-rate shapes. Rescaling return to a fixed drawdown assumes the historical maximum drawdown is the future bound and that return scales linearly with leverage; both are false, and the result is a leverage recommendation derived from the luckiest path. Both come from low-quality sources. The gated consistency criterion above does the job without these assumptions.

features.name: Composite 0-100 risk score as a control input
features.rationale: A weighted average lets one breached limit be diluted by calm components: drawdown at 100% of its limit contributes only 40 points. The weights are arbitrary and become four more parameters to fit. Driving lot size from the score adds a feedback loop between risk state and sizing that is hard to reason about and hard to test. Independent hard limits, each with its own logged block reason, are simpler and safer.

features.name: Staged optimisation switch (optimise sub-models one at a time)
features.rationale: The mechanism exists to make a many-parameter, multi-model strategy optimisable, and needing it is itself the warning sign. Sequential fitting compounds selection bias while each individual run looks modest, so the total degrees of freedom are hidden from whoever reads the final report. A survival-first v1 should have few enough parameters to be searched and validated jointly. Low-quality single source.

common_mistakes: Close-all that fires once and never checks the result: no retcode handling, no retry, no closed-versus-failed report, so the operator believes the account is flat when it is not.
Close-all utilities that close everything on the account instead of filtering by magic and symbol, killing manual trades and other EAs' positions.
Kill actions driven from OnTick, so nothing happens when no ticks arrive; conversely, assuming a button that works without ticks can also close positions while the market is shut.
Destructive buttons with no confirmation, or a MessageBox confirmation that blocks the EA while positions are open.
Kill-switch implemented only as an input flag (e.g. ShutDown.NOW): it needs the properties dialog, re-runs OnInit, and if left on it keeps closing every new trade.
Control state held only in chart objects (button state, line width, deleted arrows) and lost on timeframe change, template load or restart; no persistence of a halt.
Object names without an instance prefix and cleanup that deletes all chart objects, including the user's drawings; chart properties changed and not restored.
Manual buttons and runtime toggles that bypass the bot's risk checks or are not logged, so the live system is no longer the one that was tested.
Offering 'close profitable only' as a bulk action, which institutionalises cutting winners and holding losers.
Dashboards redrawn on every tick and left running in optimisation, slowing tests; panels that show P/L but not why trading is blocked, or show account-wide figures instead of the bot's own magic.
Alerts and push notifications raised on every tick instead of once per event, running into SendNotification rate limits.
Calling ExpertRemove() before confirming the account is flat, leaving positions with no management.
Remote control without authentication or idempotency, able to open trades, and polled in a way that blocks the trading thread.
Letting hand-drawn lines or arrows drive entries: untestable in the Strategy Tester and changed by an accidental drag.
GlobalVariable keys not scoped by account, symbol and magic, so instances overwrite each other's saved state; forgetting the four-week expiry.
Displaying 'pips' and money values with hard-coded point assumptions, which are wrong on metals where digits and contract size differ by broker and between gold and silver.

features.name: Operating-mode switch (Normal / Monitor-only / Exit-only / Flatten-and-idle)
features.rationale: A single gate is the simplest reliable manual kill-switch and gives a safe wind-down without detaching the EA, which would abandon open-trade management. MONITOR mode also allows a live dry run that can be compared with the tester. It does not touch strategy logic, so it adds no curve-fitting surface.

features.name: Independent long/short enable switches
features.rationale: Cheap operational control and a diagnostic that shows whether the edge exists on both sides. The risk is using it as an optimised parameter, so it must be fixed before testing and never tuned to the sample.

features.name: Panic flatten button with retry-until-flat and result report
features.rationale: The one manual control that directly limits loss. Most source versions fire once and never verify the result; the latched retry (48267) and the closed/failed report (62811, 67011) are what make it trustworthy. Popular (7 EAs) and in this case also worth having, provided it is scoped to the bot's own magic.

features.name: Two-step confirmation for destructive buttons
features.rationale: A flatten button with no guard will eventually be mis-clicked; a guard that blocks the EA thread is worse because stops and trailing stop being serviced. The two-click arm from 73870 costs a few lines and has neither problem.

features.name: Selective bulk close with scope selector
features.rationale: Side and pendings-only scopes are legitimate operator tools, but the full flatten already covers the emergency case, so this is not needed in v1. The profit-sign filters are common in close-all utilities and should not be carried over.

features.name: Self-removal hard stop via ExpertRemove()
features.rationale: The firmest stop available, because no bot code runs afterwards, but it also removes the dashboard and any remaining management and is undone by a simple re-attach. A persisted halt latch gives the same protection with fewer side effects, so keep this as an optional final step. In the Strategy Tester it ends the pass, which makes a breach visible instead of averaged away. Only one low-quality source.

features.name: Status dashboard with block reason and limit usage
features.rationale: An operator who cannot see why the bot is idle will override or restart it. Showing the block reason and how much of each limit is used is the minimum for supervised live running. Being read-only, it cannot make live behaviour differ from the test; it must cost nothing during optimisation.

features.name: Once-per-event alerts and push notifications
features.rationale: Risk-limit and halt events need a human quickly, and a once-per-transition alert is cheap. The sources that work remember the event index (16308) or emit from one Event() function (79372); alerting without that memory spams every tick.

features.name: News event lines and blackout label on chart
features.rationale: Explains a pause at a glance, but only has value once a news filter exists and its data can be trusted; the lines themselves change nothing. All three sources are quality-2 templates, so take the idea and not the code.

features.name: Runtime strategy overrides, per-ticket toggles and manual trade buttons
features.rationale: Every runtime override makes the live system different from the one that was tested, and the change is rarely logged, so results can no longer be attributed to the strategy. Manual entries under the bot's magic contaminate its statistics, and per-ticket toggles multiply the states to reason about. Seen in three EAs of quality 2-3; popularity here reflects manual-trader convenience, not robustness. The one good point (79285) is the shared guarded execution path.

features.name: Remote command queue with acknowledgement
features.rationale: The pattern is sound (execute once, acknowledge with the outcome), but it adds a network dependency, a blocking WebRequest, URL whitelisting and an attack surface on a live account. Worth adding later, limited to risk-reducing commands and off by default. Only one source.

features.name: User-drawn chart objects as trigger levels and direction switches
features.rationale: It makes the bot discretionary and unreproducible: hand-drawn levels cannot be backtested, state lives in fragile object properties (line width, deleted arrows), and a template change or accidental drag alters trading behaviour. Fine for a manual trader, wrong for a bot that must be honestly testable.

features.name: Manual pre-trade risk calculator (linked lines, fields and R:R)
features.rationale: A sound manual-trading aid, and its sizing arithmetic is the same the bot needs, but an automated bot sizes from its own stop distance. Keeping the panel separate keeps UI code out of the trading path. Best reference is 1637 (quality 4).

features.name: Chart markers for next trailing-stop level and broker minimum stop distance
features.rationale: Cheap diagnostic that explains skipped or rejected stop modifications. Not needed for correctness, because the stop-level check itself belongs in the execution code. One quality-2 source.

features.name: Chart hygiene: instance-scoped object names, prefix-only cleanup, restore chart
features.rationale: Basic good behaviour that prevents cross-instance bugs and stops the EA deleting the user's own drawings. It costs almost nothing if done from the first line and is painful to retrofit.

features.name: Persist operator control state across restarts
features.rationale: A kill-switch that forgets it was pressed after a restart, timeframe change or VPS reboot is not a kill-switch. The sources persist panel convenience settings; the valuable use is the halt state. Restricting persistence to control state leaves the tested parameters untouched.

features.name: Optimisation-run dashboard widgets
features.rationale: Looking at the distribution of passes is healthy, but live widgets add code with no trading value, and the tester's own results table and export already hold the data. Out of scope for v1; one source.

common_mistakes: Putting the news/trade-allowed gate in front of the whole OnTick, so stop and exit management also stop while the filter is active (19138). The gate must guard new entries only.
Matching the symbol by exact name, so broker suffixes (XAUUSDm, XAGUSD.r) silently fall back to default, non-metal settings; prefix-only matching still misses brokers that add a leading prefix.
Shipping two full hand-tuned parameter tables for gold and silver as 'presets' (both source EAs are quality 2), which doubles free parameters instead of scaling one logic by volatility.
Optimising the long side and the short side separately (duplex), which fits the trend of the test window and halves the sample behind each parameter set.
Combining signals through weighted scores, thresholds or stacked supervisor models: many correlated free parameters with no physical meaning and no way to attribute a decision.
Making signals swappable by configuration (generic iCustom adapter), which turns the EA into an indicator-shopping tool and hides repainting inputs.
Letting the EA run with invalid or inconsistent inputs instead of failing OnInit, or returning INIT_FAILED where INIT_PARAMETERS_INCORRECT would let the optimiser skip the pass.
Acting on partial data: continuing when CopyBuffer returns fewer values than requested, or when the position snapshot failed part-way through.
Treating any non-error order result as success; only DONE, DONE_PARTIAL and NO_CHANGES should count.
Rescanning positions separately inside each rule, so different rules see different state within the same tick, instead of reading one snapshot per cycle.
Driving everything from OnTick only, so management stalls in quiet markets and for symbols other than the chart symbol.
Non-idempotent management: advancing a partial-close or level counter before the close is confirmed, or handling only one level per pass so a gap through several levels is missed.
Using _Symbol/_Point/_Digits for every position in a multi-symbol EA instead of reading properties for each position's own symbol.
Sharing one magic number across sub-strategies or directions, so closes and statistics interfere; and assuming magic isolation works on netting accounts, where there is only one position per symbol.
Using one new-bar flag for all timeframes, or evaluating signals on the forming bar instead of the closed bar.
Keeping separate code for live decisions and for history/replay, which drifts apart so the backtest no longer tests what trades live.
Using a filter-combination rescoring tool to pick the best in-sample subset of filters rather than for diagnostics.
Letting an external model originate trades, calling it on every tick, or relying on a layer that cannot run in the Strategy Tester and therefore cannot be honestly backtested.
Forcing exits to mirror entry logic instead of giving exits their own independently configured conditions.
Re-entering on the same bar on which a trade series was just closed.
Creating indicator handles on every call or never releasing them, instead of caching per symbol and releasing in OnDeinit.
Scanning the whole deal history in one blocking pass on the terminal thread.
Carrying MT4/MT5 compatibility macros into a new MQL5-only bot, doubling the test surface for no benefit.
Copying architecture from low-quality EAs wholesale: more than half of these ideas come from quality 2-3 code, where the pattern is worth keeping but the implementation and numbers are not.

features.name: Signal/execution separation via narrow module interfaces
features.rationale: A clean seam lets the signal be tested with fixed risk rules and the risk/execution layer be tested with a trivial signal, so a strategy change cannot silently break order handling. It adds no tunable parameters. Build a slim own interface rather than adopting the heavy standard-library CExpert shell wholesale (268), which is opaque when something goes wrong.

features.name: One context object per symbol inside a single EA, with shared account-level risk
features.rationale: Two separate EAs cannot see each other's exposure; one EA with per-symbol objects gives a single place to cap combined risk. Caveats for honest testing: OnTick fires only for the chart symbol, so the second symbol must be serviced from the timer, and multi-symbol backtests need synchronised history for both symbols. The source EAs are quality 2, so take the structure, not the code.

features.name: Metal symbol profile with suffix-tolerant detection
features.rationale: Exact-name matching silently drops the metal settings on brokers with suffixes, and identical fixed settings mis-size silver. The risk is the opposite extreme: two full hand-tuned parameter tables double the free parameters. Both source EAs are quality 2, so adopt the detection and the idea of a minimal profile, not their numbers.

features.name: Magic-number namespace per sub-strategy and direction, with permission switches and per-magic statistics
features.rationale: Strict ownership stops the EA from touching manual trades or other EAs, and per-magic statistics let each module be judged and switched off on its own, which is what honest attribution needs. Most common architecture idea in the set, and here popularity matches merit. Magic isolation does not hold on netting accounts (one position per symbol), so the lock must be enforced there.

features.name: Duplex: fully separate long-side and short-side parameter sets and timeframes
features.rationale: It doubles the free parameters while halving the trades behind each set, and an optimised long/short asymmetry mostly memorises the drift of the test window. The cheap, useful parts (direction enable flags, separate magics) are already covered by the magic namespace feature.

features.name: Fail-fast input validation in OnInit
features.rationale: A misconfigured EA should never trade, and optimisation results should not contain nonsense passes. It is the cheapest robustness feature in the catalog and has no downside.

features.name: Unified tick-plus-timer cycle: re-entrancy guard, throttle, snapshot, idempotent actions
features.rationale: Management keeps running in quiet markets and for the non-chart symbol, repeated passes are harmless, and no rule decides from half-read or inconsistent state. The best evidence comes from the highest-quality sources in the set (79017 q5, 78821 q4). Timer behaviour in the tester depends on the tick model, so confirm that tester and live cycles behave the same.

features.name: Ordered pipeline: exits before entries, one entry gate that never blocks management
features.rationale: Reducing risk always takes priority over adding it, and a single gate gives one place to log why no trade was opened. Source 19138 put the gate in front of management as well, which leaves open positions unmanaged exactly when the filter is active; that is the mistake to design out.

features.name: Closed-bar data layer: cached indicator handles and per-timeframe new-bar gates
features.rationale: Closed-bar reads remove intrabar and repainting signals and make coarse tester modes agree with live behaviour. Cached handles avoid leaks and per-tick handle creation, and separate gates per timeframe stop one timeframe's bar event from triggering another's logic.

features.name: Single evaluator for live and replay, with a filter-result bitmask as reason code
features.rationale: One code path removes the usual drift between live logic and history/visualisation logic, and the bitmask gives honest per-filter attribution. The source also uses the bitmask to rescore every filter combination (EvalCombo); that part is a data-mining tool and should be limited to ablation checks, never to picking the best subset in-sample. Seen in only one EA, but a quality-4 one.

features.name: Trade-validator class for broker constraints, with strict retcode handling
features.rationale: Most live failures are invalid volumes, invalid stops and misread return codes. Centralising the rules removes scattered assumptions such as a hardcoded pip size, and strict success criteria stop the EA from believing an order went through when it did not.

features.name: Embedded trade-journal export at end of test and session
features.rationale: Honest testing needs raw trade records in the same format from the tester and from live trading so the two can be compared outside the terminal's summary report. The chunked incremental scan (75112) is only needed for long live histories and can come later.

features.name: Unanimous confluence of a few signal modules, with a separate exit module set
features.rationale: Unanimity adds no weights and the entry/exit decoupling is sound, but each module brings its own parameters and the on/off combination becomes another optimisable dimension. Version 1 is better served by one signal plus the entry gate; add confluence later if a single signal proves too noisy. Sources are quality 2.

features.name: Weighted-score voting with open/close thresholds, or supervisor override by specialist models
features.rationale: Scores, weights and two thresholds are correlated free parameters with no physical meaning; an optimiser will find a combination that fits any history, and individual decisions become hard to explain or attribute. The supervisor variant stacks several optimised models on top of each other. The one good idea here, different strength for entry and exit, survives in the unanimous version.

features.name: Veto-only model confirmation layer behind a deterministic pre-filter
features.rationale: The veto-only pattern is the safe way to attach any ML or LLM layer, but an external model cannot be reproduced in the Strategy Tester, so its effect cannot be honestly backtested, and a trained network (48097) carries heavy overfitting and maintenance cost. It does not belong in version 1; the base system must stand on its own without it.

features.name: Generic indicator-to-signal adapter table (config-swappable iCustom signals)
features.rationale: It exists to make indicator shopping cheap, and testing many indicator combinations until one works is the fastest route to a curve-fitted system. It also depends on external indicator binaries whose repainting behaviour the adapter cannot see, and a wrong type code or buffer index fails silently. Source is quality 2.

features.name: Macro abstraction layer for MT4/MT5 trade calls
features.rationale: Dual-platform support doubles the test surface and hides real differences in the order/position model and in tester fidelity behind macros that are hard to debug. A new MQL5-only bot gains nothing from it; the useful part, one abstraction over raw trade calls, is already delivered by the executor and validator classes.

features.name: Cross-terminal state sharing through a FILE_COMMON CSV
features.rationale: Only needed when the bot runs on more than one terminal or account. It adds a failure mode (stale or locked file) and cannot be exercised meaningfully in the tester, so it stays behind a flag with a fail-safe default. Source is a quality-2 copier; take the transport idea only.
